title: Sora 2 VidGen
content: # 🎥 Sora 2 Prompting Strategy Guide  ## Overview **Sora 2** excels with **cinematic, narrative-driven prompts** that describe **motion**, **camera movement**, and **temporal progression**.   Think like a **film director** — visualize scenes, transitions, and emotional beats.  ### 🎬 Core Concept Describe your video as if you’re **storyboarding a short film**: - Define what happens and how it’s shot. - Include camera direction, pacing, and atmosphere. - Specify transitions and key visual moments.  ---  ## 🧩 Prompt Structure Template  Use this structure for consistent, cinematic results:  [OPENING SHOT]: [Initial visual, camera position] [SUBJECT/ACTION]: [Main focus and movement] [CAMERA MOVEMENT]: [Pan, zoom, tracking, etc.] [PROGRESSION]: [How scene evolves over time] [LIGHTING/ATMOSPHERE]: [Mood, tone, and visual texture] [ENDING]: [Final frame or transition] [TECHNICAL]: [Duration, style, quality]  text  ---  ## 🎞️ Key Principles  - **Start with an establishing shot** — set the scene and visual tone.   - **Describe camera movement explicitly** — e.g., tracking, crane, dolly-in.   - **Detail subject actions over time** — show motion, reaction, or emotion.   - **Include transitions and pacing** — fade, cut, or continuous movement.   - **Build atmosphere** — lighting, sound, mood.   - **Use cinematography language** — “rack focus,” “pull back,” “soft key light.”   - **Think in sequences and beats** — define shifts or milestones in the scene.   - **Cover foreground and background activity** — adds realism and depth.  ---  ## 🧠 Example Prompts  ### ❌ Basic > "A person walking down a street."  ### ✅ Good > "A young woman in a red coat walks confidently down a bustling city street at dusk, camera follows behind her, neon signs reflecting off wet pavement."  ### 🌟 Excellent (Structured Cinematic Prompt) Opening shot: Wide angle of a rain-soaked Tokyo street at dusk, neon signs glowing in pink and blue. Subject/Action: A young woman in a vibrant red coat enters frame from the right. Camera: Smooth tracking shot, following 10 feet behind at shoulder height as she walks. Action: She navigates through the crowd with confident stride, occasionally glancing at shop windows. Her reflection appears in puddles. Progression: Camera slowly pushes in over 5 seconds, getting closer. She pauses at a crosswalk, looks up at the city skyline. Atmosphere: Moody cyberpunk aesthetic, rain creates bokeh from street lights. Steam rises from manholes. Ending: Camera continues past her as she crosses, pulling focus to blurred cityscape ahead. Technical: Duration 12s, cinematic 24fps, anamorphic lens flares, subtle film grain.  text  ---  ## 🚫 Common Mistakes  | Mistake | Description | |----------|--------------| | ❌ Static descriptions | No motion, feels like a still image | | ❌ Missing camera movement | Lacks direction or perspective | | ❌ No temporal progression | Scene doesn’t evolve or change | | ❌ Vague action verbs | "Moves around" or "does something" | | ❌ Missing duration | Sora struggles with timing | | ❌ No background context | Feels empty or flat | | ❌ Conflicting directions | Inconsistent camera or subject paths |  ---  ## ⚙️ Recommended Parameters  | Parameter | Description | Suggested Values | |------------|--------------|------------------| | **duration** | Clip length | 5–20 seconds | | **fps** | Frame rate | 24 (cinematic), 30 (smooth), 60 (high motion) | | **resolution** | Output quality | 1920×1080 (HD), 3840×2160 (4K) | | **style** | Visual tone | cinematic, documentary, experimental | | **motion_intensity** | Camera and subject dynamism | low (subtle), medium, high (dynamic) |  ---  ## 🎯 Quick Takeaway > **Think in shots, not sentences.**   Describe how the scene *starts*, *moves*, and *ends*.   Use cinematographer language to give Sora a blueprint for storytelling.

title: WAN 2.2
content: WAN 2.2 Video Prompting Guide, formatted for clarity, consistency, and quick reference in documentation or repos.  text # 🎬 WAN 2.2 Prompting Guide  ## Overview The **WAN 2.2 video model** performs best with **structured, cinematic prompts** that emphasize **storytelling**, **camera direction**, **motion cues**, and **visual style**.   For optimal consistency, keep prompts between **80–120 words** and clearly define both what happens and how it’s filmed.  ### 🎞️ Key Goals - Combine storytelling and shot design into one structured paragraph.   - Include strong **subject details**, **motion**, **visual style**, and **negatives**.   - Think like a **cinematographer** making a storyboard.  ---  ## 🧩 Prompt Structure Overview  ### 1. Subject Description Start with a vivid, detailed description of the **main subject** — appearance, pose, and intent.   > Example: *“An astronaut in a silver suit, helmet reflecting stars.”*  ### 2. Scene and Environment Set the **location, lighting, atmosphere**, or **time of day** to establish tone.   > Example: *“Floating inside a dimly lit space station, neon interface lights blinking.”*  ### 3. Motion and Camera Work Describe **how the subject and camera move** — include cinematic terms.   > Example: *“Slow-motion pan left, camera zooms in, astronaut spins weightlessly.”*  ### 4. Aesthetic and Style Modifiers Define the overall **visual treatment** and tone.   > Example: *“Cinematic lighting, shallow focus, soft bokeh, moody cyan-orange grading.”*  ### 5. Negative Prompts Specify what should **not appear** in the output.   > Example: *“–no text overlay, –no logo, –no distorted faces.”*  ---  ## 🧠 Example Frameworks  ### 🧩 Basic Formula [Subject], [Scene], [Motion/Camera], [Visual Style]  text  **Example:** > “A tabby cat leaping across a marble kitchen counter, handheld camera movement, bright morning sun streaming through the window, crisp realistic textures.”  ---  ### 🎬 Advanced / Cinematic Formula [Subject with Details], [Scene with Details], [Motion & Camera Direction], [Aesthetic/Style], [Negative Prompts]  text  **Example:** > “A woman in flowing red silk, standing on a windswept rooftop in a futuristic city at dusk, slow dolly-in shot, billowing fabric, dramatic golden-hour lighting, shallow depth of field –no watermark, –no text overlay.”  ---  ## ⚙️ Technical & Performance Tips  - Keep prompts **80–120 words** for ideal control and balance.   - Always describe **camera setup** and how it **evolves over time**.     > Example: *“Begins with a wide shot above the city, then a crane shot lowers to the subject’s face.”*   - Use **motion cues** — speed, direction, parallax, or character actions.     > Example: *“Whip-pan left, hair moves in slow motion.”*   - Include **style tags** for lighting, color, or lens effects.     > Example: *“Anamorphic bokeh, 16mm grain, golden-hour tone.”*   - Explicitly list **negative prompts** to suppress unwanted artifacts.   - For **I2V (image-to-video)** workflows, describe how the motion evolves from the base frame.     > Example: *“Character blinks and tilts head as camera arcs right.”*  ---  ## 🎥 Key Cinematic Vocabulary  | Category | Terms | |-----------|-------| | **Camera** | pan, tilt, dolly, orbital, crane, POV, tracking, aerial, close-up, wide shot | | **Lighting** | soft, harsh, rim, volumetric, neon, golden hour, diffuse backlight | | **Styles** | vintage film, CGI, line art, hyperreal, fantasy | | **Motion** | slow-motion, time-lapse, still, fast, dynamic |  ---  ## 🎯 Quick Takeaway > **WAN 2.2 rewards precision.**   Structure prompts like a film scene — define what happens, how it moves, and how it feels.   Always include motion, camera direction, style tags, and negatives for full control.

title: Kling O1
content: For Kling O1, “right context” basically means giving the model a clean, director-style instruction that covers subject, action/motion, environment, look, and camera, plus how they should evolve over the clip.​  Core prompt structure for O1 A reliable pattern that aligns with Kling’s own guides and the newer O1 tutorials is:  [Shot / camera] – shot type or movement  [Subject + appearance] – who/what, key visual traits  [Action / motion] – how subject moves over time  [Environment] – place, time of day, weather, background  [Lighting + style + mood] – look and vibe of the footage  Example pattern (fill in your specifics): “Medium tracking shot of [subject description] [doing action] in [environment], [lighting], [visual style], [mood].”​  This matches Kling’s recommended breakdown of: subject → subject description → subject movement → scene/environment → optional camera, lighting, style.​  Text-to-video context When starting from pure text (no refs), make the prompt about motion and relationships over time, not just static looks.​  Start with subject and action: “A young woman in business casual walking quickly through a busy subway station…”  Then add camera: “…handheld camera following from behind, slight shake, occasional rack focus to the crowd.”  Then add environment and light: “…fluorescent lighting, cool tones, reflective tiles, rush-hour crowd.”  This “big picture → style → motion” flow is consistent with current Kling text-to-video prompt frameworks.​  Image / multi-image context For O1’s image and multi-image modes, treat the images as hard visual context and the prompt as motion + cinematic intent.​  Use refs for identity, outfit, product, environment, etc.  Use prompt to specify:  What moves (subject, camera, or both)  How it moves (slow pan, push-in, orbit, dolly, etc.)  Temporal beats: “starts on wide establishing shot, then slowly pushes into close-up on the product.”  You can also define start and end frame behavior by focusing your text on what should happen between these frames: “From start frame to end frame, the character walks toward camera while the background defocuses and sun flares grow stronger.”​  Video-to-video / edit context For edit mode, Kling O1 expects prompts that respect the existing motion and composition and only redefine what should change: style, subject class, background, weather, clothing, etc.​  Good pattern: “Keep the same timing and camera movement. Turn the office into a neon cyberpunk bar, change the man’s suit into a black leather jacket, add rainy reflections on the floor, cinematic teal and orange grading.”  Avoid re-specifying totally different blocking or camera if you want motion preserved; frame it as restyle/replace.​  Practical “right context” tips Think like a DP, not a novelist: short, concrete instructions > long prose.​  Prioritize constraints: subject, motion, camera, environment; style words come last.​  Don’t overload: 1–2 actions, 1 clear camera behavior, 1 environment. Too many beats leads to muddy outputs.​  Use consistent naming: if using multiple refs (“girl A”, “girl B”, “red sports car”), keep the same labels in the prompt so O1 can track entities.​

Camera & Motion Design  ### 4.1 Camera Framing - **Shot type:** Wide, medium, close‑up, POV, over‑the‑shoulder   - **Angle:** Eye level, low angle, high angle, overhead   - **Lens feel (optional):** Wide, normal, telephoto vibe    ### 4.2 Camera Movement - **Move description:** Slow pan, push‑in, pull‑back, orbit, tracking   - **Move path & timing:** e.g., start wide → push‑in over full 10s, end on face   - **Stability:** Tripod‑steady, subtle handheld, no shake    ### 4.3 Subject vs Camera Motion - **Subject motion:** What moves, how fast, how much   - **Camera motion:** Fixed, gentle push‑in, fast dynamic move   - **Emphasis:** Prioritize subject performance or environment reveal    ---  ## 5. Audio & Dialogue  ### 5.1 Character Dialogue (Native Audio) - **Speaker tag + line:**     `"CHARACTER: "Exact line of dialogue here."`   - **Delivery:** Calm, nervous, excited, whispering, robotic   - **Language & accent (if needed)**    ### 5.2 Ambient & FX - **Background bed:** City hum, forest birds, rain, crowd murmur   - **Foreground SFX:** Footsteps, rustling clothes, typing, engine, doors   - **Mix focus:** Dialogue forward, ambience dominant, balanced    ### 5.3 Music (If Desired) - **Type:** Atmospheric synths, orchestral strings, lo‑fi beat   - **Mood:** Tense build, uplifting, melancholic   - **Placement:** Throughout, only intro, only ending    ---  ## 6. title: WAN 2.2 s2v
content: Wan2.2-S2V gives you two “levers”: the audio + reference image drive timing, lip‑sync and micro‑motion, while your text prompt and workflow settings control style, framing, and macro motion.[](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/artificial-intelligence/audio-driven-videogen/README.html)​  ## Core inputs to control  Wan2.2-S2V uses four inputs that each control different aspects of the video:[](https://github.com/Wan-Video/Wan2.2)​  - Image: Locks in character look, clothing, and base composition.      - Audio: Drives mouth shapes, head/hand beats, and expression over time.      - Text prompt (optional but recommended): Sets scene, style, camera behavior, and non‑speech actions.      - Pose video (optional): Adds body/gesture motion patterns, especially for full‑body or performance shots.[](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/artificial-intelligence/audio-driven-videogen/README.html)​       ## Prompt structure for S2V  Treat the S2V prompt as “global direction” rather than a storyboard. Keep it compact and cinematic. A good structure:[](https://www.mimicpc.com/learn/how-to-craft-wan22-ai-video-prompts)​  - Subject and role: “close‑up of a 30‑year‑old woman, tech founder, talking to camera”      - Setting and mood: “in a modern office at night, soft warm key light, dark background, cinematic, shallow depth of field”      - Camera behavior: “static camera, fixed lens, no camera shake” (or “slow dolly in”, “subtle handheld”, etc.)      - Motion constraints: “minimal head movement, natural blinking, slight hand gestures in frame”       Avoid describing exact syllable‑level actions (“she nods on every word”) – those conflict with audio control and cause jitter.[](https://comfyui-wiki.com/en/tutorial/advanced/video/wan2.2/wan2-2-s2v)​  ## Negative prompting and over‑control  Use a short negative prompt to suppress unwanted artifacts, not to micromanage movement. Examples:[](https://comfyui-wiki.com/en/tutorial/advanced/video/wan2.2/wan2-2-s2v)​  - “blurry, deformed face, extra limbs, warped mouth, out of frame, text, logo, watermark”      - If it over‑gestures: “exaggerated hand movements, excessive head wobble”       Keep both positive and negative prompts reasonably short; S2V tends to ignore late‑prompt clauses if you go essay‑length.[](https://www.reddit.com/r/StableDiffusion/comments/1mc67xp/wan22_prompting_guide/)​  ## ComfyUI workflow levers  In the ComfyUI S2V workflows:[](https://comfyanonymous.github.io/ComfyUI_examples/wan22/)​  - Positive/negative conditioning go into the Wan S2V node and then into the sampler, same as T2V/I2V.      - Steps / CFG scale: higher CFG enforces prompt style harder but can fight the audio‑driven motion; if you see “snappy” or off‑beat lips, lower CFG a bit.      - Duration / fps: S2V tracks the whole audio; long audios with very low fps can smear facial motion.       If you use the “Fun Camera” / camera embedding workflows with S2V, set camera motion in the WanCameraEmbedding node (zoom, pan, static, speed) and keep prompt camera language consistent with that choice.[](https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/video/wan/wan2-2-fun-camera)​  ## Practical prompting patterns  A few patterns that tend to work well across S2V use cases:​[](https://www.mimicpc.com/learn/how-to-craft-wan22-ai-video-prompts)​  - Direct‑to‑camera talk: “medium close‑up, static camera, eye‑level shot, natural corporate interview lighting, speaker looking into camera, subtle breathing, cinematic 4k.”      - Podcast / YouTube: “three‑quarter view, soft key light from the left, bokeh background with neon lights, gentle handheld camera, casual expressive hand gestures.”      - Singing / performance: “full‑body shot on stage, dynamic colored spotlights, energetic but controlled body movement, smooth camera dolly left to right.”       If you describe camera movement in the prompt, avoid contradicting it with nodes (e.g., prompt says “static” but camera embedding is “zoom in”) to keep motion stable.[](https://www.reddit.com/r/comfyui/comments/1mbmdqy/wan22_prompt_guide_update_camera_movement/)​

title: LTX 2.3
content: You can think of LTX‑2.3 prompts as short “shot descriptions” that always cover six core elements in one flowing paragraph: shot, scene, action, character, camera, and audio. ​  Core structure for LTX‑2.3 prompts Use this mental template for every cinematic clip you write: ​  Shot type and style  Name the shot and vibe: “wide establishing shot”, “intimate close‑up”, “handheld thriller scene”, “documentary style”. ​  Mention genre if relevant: “neo‑noir”, “period drama”, “epic fantasy”, “documentary”. ​  Scene and atmosphere  Describe time of day, location, lighting, color, and atmosphere in concrete terms:  “golden‑hour sunlight, long soft shadows, warm orange and teal palette, light fog in the distance, wet asphalt reflecting neon signs”. ​  Include textures (“worn leather jacket, rough brick walls, glossy puddles”) and weather (rain, fog, dust, smoke, particles). ​  Action over time (beginning → middle → end)  Write the action as a continuous sequence in present tense: what happens first, then, and at the end. ​  Specify who moves, what moves, and how: “she slowly steps forward”, “cars glide past”, “leaves swirl in the wind”. ​  Avoid static, photo‑like descriptions; always include verbs and evolving motion. ​  Character description and emotion as behavior  Add concise casting‑style details: age range, gender expression, clothing, hair, key features. ​  Show emotion via physical cues, not labels:  Instead of “she is sad”, write “her shoulders slump, eyes glassy, jaw clenched as she avoids the camera”.  Camera language  Explicitly direct the camera using film terms:  “slow dolly‑in toward his face”, “handheld tracking shot as the camera follows behind”, “camera circles around them in a 120‑degree arc”, “crane up then settle into a medium shot”.  Tie camera moves to moments in the action (“as he opens the door, the camera pushes in”). ​  Audio description (optional but powerful)  Describe ambient sound, music, and any dialogue. Place dialogue in quotation marks. ​  Include tone and mix: “soft piano and distant traffic hum”, “low ominous drone with muffled thunder”. ​  For voices, mention style and intensity: “calm, resonant narrator”, “excited reporter shouting over the crowd”. ​  Formatting and length Write as a single, flowing paragraph, 4–8 sentences long. ​  Use present tense throughout (“the camera moves”, “she walks”). ​  Match detail level to shot scale: close‑ups need more face and micro‑gesture detail; wides need environment and blocking. ​  Keep logic clean: consistent lighting, a small number of characters, and non‑contradictory instructions. ​  Cinematic “ingredient list” you can reuse You can mix and match these phrases while keeping the paragraph format:  Camera: “slow dolly‑in”, “steady tripod shot”, “handheld tracking”, “over‑the‑shoulder”, “wide establishing shot”, “overhead view”, “camera circles around”, “pushes in / pulls back”. ​  Lighting: “neon glow”, “flickering candlelight”, “harsh fluorescent”, “soft golden‑hour backlight”, “dramatic chiaroscuro shadows”. ​  Film look: “natural film grain”, “anamorphic lens with oval bokeh and gentle lens flares”, “high‑contrast black and white”, “muted, desaturated color palette”.  Pacing: “slow motion”, “lingering continuous shot”, “time‑lapse feeling of clouds racing by”. ​  Atmosphere: “light rain and rising steam”, “dust motes in the sunlight”, “thick morning fog rolling over the hills”. ​  Example prompt pattern for LTX‑2.3 Here is a reusable pattern you can adapt for any cinematic clip:  Wide establishing shot of [location] at [time of day], [lighting and color palette] with [atmospheric details] in the air. A [brief character description] stands/sits/moves in the foreground, [clothing, posture, and key behavior that shows emotion]. The camera [describe initial camera position], then [describe how it moves: tracks, dollies, orbits] as [describe what the character and environment do over time]. In the background, [secondary motion: traffic, waves, trees, crowd] adds subtle movement without stealing focus. Ambient sound of [environment] blends with [music description], while the [character or narrator] says, “[…]” in a [voice style and intensity] voice. The shot ends as [soft closing action that naturally resolves the motion].

title: Veo 3.1 VidGen
content: Core mental model for Veo 3.1 i2v Think: “I already have the frame; I’m just directing how it moves over 8 seconds.” The image supplies subject, style, and setting. ​  Your prompt should focus on:  Camera behavior (pan, tilt, dolly, zoom, orbit).  What moves and how (character actions, environment changes, FX).  Optional audio (ambience, SFX, music cues).  A useful base formula for Veo 3.1 i2v is: [Camera] + [Action / Motion] + [Timing & Duration] + [Audio].  Example for a single still keyframe: “Slow dolly-in toward the woman’s face as her hair and coat gently move in the wind, background city lights subtly twinkling over 8 seconds, quiet street ambience with distant traffic and soft wind.”  Modes and keyframe guidance Plain i2v (single start frame):  You pass one image (start frame); prompt describes how the scene evolves from that image over N seconds.  Best for: light character motion, subtle camera parallax, environmental movement, logo/product animations.  First/Last frame (keyframe control):  You pass first image directly and last image as a constraint in config; Veo interpolates between them.  Prompt should describe the transition path: what morphs, what stays rigid, how the camera travels between A and B, and any temporal beats (halfway, final second, etc.).  Example transition prompt: “Begin on the wide shot of the empty classroom, then the camera slowly dollies forward and slightly tilts up as lights warm up and dust particles become visible in a sunbeam, arriving on the final close-up composition by second 8, with soft room tone and faint kids’ laughter echoing in the distance.”  Segmenting prompts for modular control Veo ultimately receives a single text prompt for the clip, so your modular/LLM system should “compile” segments into one coherent shot description with embedded timing.  A practical pattern:  Define a per-shot JSON schema (what your upstream LLMs/nodes will fill):  json {   "shot_id": "shot_03",   "duration_seconds": 8,   "camera": {     "movement": "slow dolly-in with slight handheld sway",     "path": "from medium-wide to tight medium on subject",     "notes": "no whip pans or sudden moves"   },   "motion": {     "primary_subject": "man in hoodie slowly turning toward camera",     "secondary": "neon signs flicker subtly, light rain falling",     "intensity_curve": "very subtle at start, most noticeable in last 2 seconds"   },   "transition": {     "mode": "first_last_frame",     "from_frame": "kf_03_start.png",     "to_frame": "kf_03_end.png",     "description": "background parallax and lighting shift, character pose rotates 45 degrees"   },   "audio": {     "generate_audio": true,     "ambience": "city at night, distant traffic, muffled crowd",     "music": "low-key synth pad, no percussion"   },   "style_lock": "strictly preserve existing color grade, film grain, and lens bokeh from keyframe" } Have a “prompt compiler” template that turns that JSON into Veo-ready text, e.g.:  “8-second shot. Slow dolly-in with slight handheld sway, moving from a medium-wide to a tight medium on the man in a hoodie, preserving the existing color grade, film grain, and bokeh from the keyframe. The man slowly turns about 45 degrees toward the camera while neon signs behind him flicker subtly and light rain falls. Motion is very subtle at first and becomes most noticeable in the last 2 seconds. The camera ends in the exact final composition of the provided last frame. Audio: city-at-night ambience with distant traffic and a muffled crowd, plus a low-key synth pad without percussion. Generate audio.”  You can keep your internal prompt modular (camera, motion, transition, audio) while always emitting one clean, linear description per clip for Veo.  Technical knobs you should always set Most Veo 3.1 i2v APIs expose similar config fields:  Duration: 4–8 seconds (8 is typical default).  Resolution: 720p or 1080p; some providers support 4K for certain tiers.  Aspect ratio: usually 16:9, 9:16, 1:1, possibly others depending on host.  Audio: boolean flag to generate audio or keep silent.  In a Node/JS-style call (e.g., Gemini API flavor), your pipeline will look like:  ts const operation = await ai.models.generateVideos({   model: "veo-3.1-generate-preview",   prompt: compiledPrompt,         // from your modular system   image: startFrame,              // first keyframe   config: {     lastFrame,                    // optional end keyframe for interpolation     durationSeconds: 8,     resolution: "1080p",     aspectRatio: "16:9",     generateAudio: true   } }); Guardrails and failure modes Don’t re-describe the image (“A man in a hoodie at night city street”) if it’s already clearly visible; it can introduce conflicts.  Avoid multi-subject or multi-location instructions in a single 8-second i2v shot (e.g., “he walks from the city to a forest to a beach”); split into separate clips instead.  Be explicit about things that must not change: “keep framing and lens distortion identical to the keyframe,” “do not change wardrobe or background design.”  If you share one example keyframe plus a target action (e.g., “news/doc hero shot, 8s, subtle moves”), I can write a handful of concrete Veo 3.1 i2v prompt templates that you can drop straight into your n8n/ComfyUI prompt compiler—does that help?

title: Sora 2 Pro VidGen
content: # 🎬 Sora 2 Pro Prompting Guide  ## Overview **Sora 2 Pro** is OpenAI’s premium video generation model built for structured, cinematic storytelling.  ### Key Features - Supports **15,000+ characters (~3,000 tokens)**   - **Synced audio** (dialogue, music, SFX)   - **Face cameos** (upload images for lip-sync dialogue)   - **Longer clips** up to **25 seconds**   - Excels with **storyboard-style prompts**  💡 **Tip:** Treat your prompt like a **storyboard script** — describe shots sequentially with details on camera work, lighting, mood, actions, and audio.  ---  ## 🧩 Prompt Structure  Each Sora Pro prompt works best when broken into four clear sections:  ### 1. Subject / Environment Describe the scene and primary subject in vivid detail.   > Example: *“Majestic sea turtle with barnacle-covered shell in crystal-clear turquoise waters.”*  ### 2. Cinematography / Mood Define the style, framing, and tone of the shot.   > Example: *“Low-angle tracking shot, golden hour, moody chiaroscuro lighting.”*  ### 3. Action Sequence List each movement or moment as numbered steps to preserve clarity.   > Example:   > 1. Turtle turns head   > 2. Flipper stroke exits frame  ### 4. Audio Include ambient sound, music, or dialogue as part of the shot description.   > Example: *“Distant whale calls, sweeping orchestral score.”*  ---  ## ⚙️ Best Practices  - **Balance detail:** Enough to control visuals, but not so dense that creativity is lost.   - **Iterate deliberately:** Start tweaks with camera and lighting before reworking narrative or pacing.   - **Pro workflows:**     - Upload face images for cameo dialogue matching.     - Reference prior shots for multi-scene continuity.   - **Avoid pitfalls:**     - One major action per shot.     - Avoid vague language ("beautiful shot," "nice lighting").     - Always specify visual tone or medium (e.g., *"IMAX epic," "16mm documentary"*).   - **Length guidance:**     - Focus on the first **500 characters** for strongest influence.     - Handles **2k–15k+ characters** reliably.  ---  ## 🧠 Example Prompts  ### 🎥 Product Reveal Cinematic unboxing of premium mirrorless camera on wooden table. Slow dolly in (0–3s), warm morning light; hands open box (3–8s), foley clicks; profile reveal (8–12s), lens flare. VO (female, calm): "Meet the focus of your next story." Room tone + shutter SFX.  text  ### 🎭 Emotional Close-up elderly woman’s hands on piano; reflection shows younger self. Slow rack focus, soft lighting. Ambient piano melody.  text  ### 👤 Cameo Use uploaded face: avatar steps into cozy living room, sits, greets "Hey—welcome back!" (warm voice). Kettle hum, vinyl crackle.  text  ---  ## 🪄 Quick Reference  | Section | Purpose | Example | |----------|----------|----------| | **Subject/Environment** | Define setting & main subject | “Sea turtle in turquoise ocean” | | **Cinematography/Mood** | Describe shot type & tone | “Low-angle, golden hour lighting” | | **Action Sequence** | Stepwise movement | “1. Turns head; 2. Swims away” | | **Audio** | Sound, music, dialogue | “Whale calls, orchestral score” |  ---  ### 🧰 Pro Tip When refining prompts, imagine **directing the scene**—the clearer your camera, emotion, and pacing, the more cinematic your output will feel.  ---

title: Seedance v1.5 Pro
content: Seedance 1.5 Pro is ByteDance’s joint audio‑video text/image‑to‑video model, so its “prompting context” is mainly a structured text description plus a few control parameters (duration, aspect ratio, camera, audio) that drive both visuals and sound together.  Core prompting context Input types: Text‑to‑video (prompt only) and image‑to‑video (reference image + prompt).  What the prompt controls: Subject, actions/motion, environment, camera behavior, and any explicit audio/dialogue or sound cues you describe.  Audio–video joint generation: The same prompt is used to synthesize video and synchronized audio in one pass, so wording about speech, music, or SFX directly shapes the soundtrack and lip‑sync.  Recommended prompt structure Most official and third‑party guides converge on a layered or slot‑based structure:  Subject: who/what is onscreen (age, clothing, style, species, etc.).  Motion/action: what they do over the clip (walks, turns, speaks, dances, reacts).  Scene/background: location, time of day, lighting, style (cinematic, anime, clay, etc.).  Camera: shot type and motion (close‑up, tracking shot, slow zoom out, orbit, fixed).  Audio/dialogue: language, tone, content of speech, music genre, ambient sounds, emotional delivery.  Example style (compressed from docs): “Close‑up of an elderly man telling a heartfelt story at sunset, warm golden‑hour light, slow camera push‑in, soft piano music, his voice is calm and emotional in English.”  Key API‑level context Typical text‑to‑video parameters exposed by providers (names vary slightly per host):  Concept	Typical field / effect Concept	Typical field / effect Prompt	prompt – required text description. ​ Duration	duration 4–12 s, -1 for “smart duration”. ​ Ratio	ratio or aspect_ratio, or adaptive. Resolution	resolution 480p or 720p, some UIs upscale. Camera fixed	fixed_camera / camera_fixed boolean. Seed	seed integer, -1 or null for random. Generate audio	generate_audio or similar toggle. Negative prompts are generally unnecessary or ignored; guidance is to describe what you want, not what to avoid.  Behavioral characteristics Joint AV model: Dual‑branch diffusion transformer (MMDiT/DB‑DiT) with ~4.5B params, generating 1080p up to ~12 seconds at 24 fps.  Strengths: Tight lip‑sync, rich ambient/foley, robust camera motion, and solid instruction following for multi‑part actions.  Best practice: Keep prompts concise but specific; emphasize moving parts, camera, and audio cues rather than static decoration text. title: Flux 1 Kontext
content: You can think of FLUX.1 Kontext as “describe edits like a director giving instructions on set,” and it will handle composition, lighting, and character consistency for you.  What FLUX.1 Kontext Actually Does It is a flow‑matching model that unifies text‑to‑image and image editing: you can start from scratch or feed one or more reference images plus text instructions.  It’s built for in‑context generation: it reads the context image(s) and your instruction together, then produces a new view that respects identity, layout, and style.  Key strengths you can lean on in prompts: character consistency, targeted local edits, style transfer from references, and fast multi‑turn iteration with little drift.  General Prompt Structure For Cinematic Shots Black Forest Labs’ own guidance for FLUX models recommends a structured prompt: Subject + Action + Style + Context. For cinematic imagery with Kontext, that becomes:  Subject: who/what is on camera (one clear subject works best for quality and consistency).  Action / pose: what they’re doing, body orientation, camera angle (close‑up, medium shot, wide, over‑the‑shoulder).  Cinematic style: film look (e.g., “anamorphic lens bokeh”, “35mm film grain”, “desaturated neo‑noir”), depth of field, aspect ratio hints.  Scene context: time of day, location, weather, background blocking (foreground / midground / background) and mood.  Example base prompt (text‑to‑image):  “Young woman in a rain‑soaked Tokyo alley at night, medium shot, facing camera, neon reflections on wet pavement, shallow depth of field, cinematic lighting, subtle 35mm film grain, anamorphic bokeh, moody blue‑and‑magenta color grade, high dynamic range, 16:9 frame”  This follows the subject‑first, foundation‑before‑decoration pattern that Flux models respond to well.  Using Kontext’s Image Input For Cinematic Edits Because Kontext is built to concatenate context image tokens with your instruction, it is very good at “keep these things, change those things.”  When editing an existing still toward a cinematic look:  Clearly state what must be preserved.  “Keep her face, hairstyle, and outfit exactly as in the reference, same framing.”  Then give the cinematic transformation.  “Turn this into a dramatic nighttime street‑scene still from a prestige TV drama, strong backlight rim on hair, subtle smoke in background, shallow depth of field, rich contrast, teal‑and‑orange color grade.”  For local edits, identify the region and the cinematic intent.  “Only change the background: replace the plain wall with a blurred city skyline at dusk, bokeh lights, keep subject lighting consistent with sunset.”  For multi‑turn workflows, repeat preservation language.  Kontext is designed to keep characters stable across many edits, but you still help it by reiterating which aspects must not change on each turn.  Cinematic Elements To Explicitly Control When you “gather context” for cinematic prompting, build a small checklist you always cover in the instruction. FLUX‑style guides emphasize being precise and hierarchical, not piling random adjectives at the end.  Camera and framing: close‑up, extreme close‑up, medium shot, wide shot, low angle, high angle, over‑the‑shoulder, tracking‑shot feel.  Lens and depth of field: “shallow depth of field, subject sharp, background heavily blurred, anamorphic bokeh, 85mm portrait lens look.”  Lighting: key light direction, intensity, and quality: “hard top‑down fluorescent,” “soft window light from the left,” “strong backlight with silhouette edges,” “high‑contrast chiaroscuro.”  Color grade: “cool blue‑gray, desaturated”, “warm amber tungsten”, “teal‑and‑orange blockbuster grade”, “muted earth‑tones like a period drama.”  Production design: era, wardrobe, environment clutter, smoke, rain, dust, lens flares, reflections, etc.  Foreground / midground / background: FLUX.1 specifically benefits when you describe what belongs in each layer instead of mixing them.  Example instruction for an edit:  “Keep the couple and their pose exactly as in the photo. Transform the scene into a cinematic nighttime city rooftop, medium‑wide shot, camera slightly below eye level. Add soft practical lights in the background, shallow depth of field, gentle lens flare from an off‑screen neon sign, subtle grain and a teal‑and‑orange color grade like a modern romantic drama.”  Practical Prompt Patterns And Pitfalls Based on Flux‑focused prompt guides and hands‑on usage notes, a few patterns matter a lot for Kontext.  Patterns that work well  One main subject per frame for higher quality and consistency; add others only when necessary.  Short, direct instructions for edits: “remove…”, “replace… with…”, “make this look like…”, “only change…”.  Iterative refinement: first get framing and pose right, then run follow‑up edits for lighting, mood, and small details.  Reusing the same reference image(s) in multi‑turn workflows to stabilize characters across different cinematic scenes.  Things to avoid or adjust  Overloaded, unordered prompts (e.g., mixing foreground/background demands mid‑sentence) – instead, group them clearly: “foreground… midground… background…”.  Conflicting style cues like “anime style, ultra‑realistic cinematic still” in the same sentence; pick one dominant cinematic style.  Vague directions like “make it more epic” without concrete film‑language changes (angle, scale, lighting, environment)

title: WAN 2.7
content: Wan 2.7 is designed specifically for cinematic‑style video generation, with strong support for image‑to‑video, first‑frame/last‑frame (keyframe 1 → keyframe 2), and multi‑shot workflows. To write effective cinematic prompts you need to bake in scene language, motion, and camera direction while staying compatible with how Wan 2.7 interprets prompts.  Below is the core context you should internalize for prompt‑writing, then I’ll follow up with concrete prompt templates you can reuse.  What Wan 2.7 can do Image‑to‑video: Take a single still as a starting frame and animate it with motion, camera moves, and subtle continuity.  First/last frame control: Define both the opening and closing frame; Wan 2.7 interpolates the motion path between them, which is exactly “keyframe 1 → keyframe 2” storytelling.  9‑grid / multi‑shot: Use a 3×3 grid of stills to build a sequence of scenes that are stitched into one continuous, cinematic clip.  Subject + voice references: Lock character identity and optionally match voice or emotional tone across shots.  How prompts are structured in Wan 2.7 Most guides and the official Wan 2.7 prompt recipe treat the prompt as a two‑part structure:  Motion description:  What is moving and how (e.g., “a knight slowly walks forward”, “raindrops fall diagonally”).  Use adverbs to control speed and intensity: “slowly”, “sharply”, “smoothly”, “violently”.  Camera movement:  Explicit cinematic camera terms: “dolly in”, “pull back”, “low‑angle shot”, “orbital camera”, “handheld jitter”, “static shot”.  You can also specify lens behavior: “shallow depth of field”, “wide‑angle lens”, “cinematic shallow focus”.  This “motion + camera” pairing is what makes prompts feel like filmic directions rather than a bland description.  Cinematic “ingredients” to include in a prompt When you aim for cinematic prompts for image‑to‑video or keyframe‑to‑keyframe, consistently add:  Scene setting: Time of day, weather, and environment (e.g., “sunset over a cyberpunk city”, “misty forest at dawn”).  Lighting & mood:  “cinematic neon lighting”, “volumetric fog”, “high‑contrast chiaroscuro”, “golden hour glow”.  Composition notes:  “wide shot”, “close‑up”, “medium shot”, “over‑the‑shoulder”, “hero framing”, “rule of thirds”.  Pacing and motion:  “slow, deliberate push‑in”, “dynamic tracking shot”, “rapid cuts between frames”, “smooth, fluid motion”.  For keyframe‑controlled clips, you also want to hint at the transition between frames:  “the camera starts on a close‑up of the character’s face, then slowly pulls back to reveal a vast battlefield”  “the scene transitions from a dimly lit room to a bright sunlit street, with the character walking forward”  Special modes for your use cases Image‑to‑video (single frame start):  Start with a strong visual description of the input image, then add the motion and camera.  Example structure:  [image description]  then [motion description]  camera [camera move].  Keyframe 1 → keyframe 2 (first/last frame):  Describe both endpoints clearly within the prompt, even if you already upload the frames.  Example pattern:  “The video starts with [keyframe 1 description] and ends with [keyframe 2 description], with smooth camera motion and natural lighting transitions.”  9‑grid / sequence‑based:  Treat each panel as a mini‑scene and describe the chain of events:  “Panel 1: [scene A]; the camera pans to reveal Panel 2: [scene B]; then the shot continues to Panel 3: [scene C], and so on.”  Prompt archetypes you can reuse Once you have this context, you can build a small library of prompt “templates” for your workflow. For example:  Image‑to‑cinematic shot:  “A [subject] in [setting], cinematic lighting, slow dolly in as the [subject] [motion], shallow depth of field, subtle camera shake, 4K cinematic.”  Keyframe transition (1 → 2):  “Start in [keyframe 1 description], then [motion/transition], ending in [keyframe 2 description], smooth camera move, cinematic color grading, natural motion blur.”  Pull‑back / reveal sequence:  “Close‑up of [detached detail], then camera slowly pulls back to reveal [the full scene] as [additional motion occurs], wide‑angle cinematic shot.”

title: Seedance v2.0
content: You are a cinematic prompt enhancer for Seedance 2.0 video generation.  Your job is to turn a short, simple user prompt into a strong, concise cinematic prompt that works well for reference image and reference video workflows.  Rules:  Preserve the user’s original subject, action, and intent.  Add cinematic detail without changing the meaning.  Make the prompt visual and production-oriented.  Optimize for video generation, not still images.  Emphasize motion, camera behavior, lighting, atmosphere, composition, and mood.  If the user provides a reference image, keep identity, outfit, scene layout, and style continuity stable.  If the user provides a reference video, preserve the motion pattern, timing, and camera logic while improving visual quality or style.  Do not add new story elements unless they clearly support the original prompt.  Avoid overly long prompts; aim for vivid but efficient language.  Prefer concrete film language over vague adjectives.  Include constraints when useful, such as: smooth motion, natural anatomy, stable face, no flicker, no warping, no jitter.  When enhancing a prompt, use this structure:  Subject and action.  Scene and environment.  Camera movement.  Lighting and color mood.  Visual style and cinematic treatment.  Quality and stability constraints.  Style guidance:  Use filmic terms like: wide shot, close-up, tracking shot, dolly-in, slow push, shallow depth of field, soft rim light, golden hour, volumetric light, atmospheric haze, dramatic contrast, handheld realism, smooth motion.  Keep the prompt grounded and visually specific.  If the source prompt is generic, make it feel like a real shot from a film or premium commercial.  If the source prompt is already detailed, refine and tighten it rather than adding clutter.  Output format:  Return only the enhanced cinematic prompt.  Do not explain your changes.  Do not include analysis or bullet points unless the user explicitly asks for them.  Example transformations:  Simple: “a woman walking in the street”  Enhanced: “A stylish woman walking down a city street at dusk, confident pace, cinematic tracking shot, soft neon reflections on wet pavement, shallow depth of field, moody urban atmosphere, smooth natural motion, realistic face and body movement.”  Simple: “a dog running on the beach”  Enhanced: “A joyful dog sprinting along the shoreline at sunset, low-angle tracking shot, golden hour light, ocean spray, wind moving through fur, wide cinematic composition, smooth motion, natural physics, vivid but realistic color grading.”  Simple: “a car driving at night”  Enhanced: “A sleek car driving through the city at night, slow moving tracking shot, glowing streetlights reflecting across the bodywork, rain-slick asphalt, neon highlights, dramatic contrast, cinematic motion blur, polished commercial look.”

title: Chroma 1
content: Master template Use this as your base:  “A [subject] in [environment], [action or pose], with [key visual details]. The scene is lit by [lighting description], creating [mood]. Frame it as a [shot type] with [lens feel or depth of field], [color palette], and [finish].”  Negative prompt: “blurry, low detail, deformed hands, distorted face, flat lighting, noisy background, text, watermark”  Portrait template For portraits, keep the subject simple and the light controlled. Chroma examples show that strong results often come from explicit portrait framing, lens choice, and lighting direction.  “A cinematic close-up portrait of a [person description], wearing [wardrobe], with [expression]. Soft directional light from [side], gentle background blur, shallow depth of field, and subtle skin texture. The image feels polished, dramatic, and intimate, with a restrained [color palette].”  Negative prompt: “bad anatomy, asymmetrical face, extra fingers, plastic skin, harsh flash, blur, oversaturated colors”  Action template Action prompts should describe motion, energy, and camera perspective clearly. Diffusion prompt guides recommend specifying the event, location, and visual motion cues rather than using broad words like “epic”.  “A cinematic action scene of [subject] [doing something dynamic] in [location]. Motion blur trails, dust or rain in the air, dramatic rim light, and a low-angle shot that emphasizes scale. High contrast, sharp subject separation, and a tense, film-still atmosphere.”  Negative prompt: “motion smear on face, duplicate limbs, broken perspective, washed-out lighting, cluttered background”  Landscape template For landscapes, lead with the environment, weather, and atmosphere. Chroma landscape examples emphasize wide framing, strong horizon design, and readable light sources.  “A wide cinematic landscape of [place], with [terrain details], [weather], and [time of day]. Light spills across the scene in [lighting description], with atmospheric haze, strong depth, and a natural color gradient. Shot as an expansive vista with crisp detail and a calm, immersive mood.”  Negative prompt: “flat horizon, muddy colors, low contrast, haze blocking detail, warped trees, oversharpened rocks”  Fast recipe If you want better results quickly, follow this sequence: subject first, then setting, then light, then camera, then finish. Chroma documentation also notes that higher guidance pushes the image closer to the prompt, while overly strong guidance can reduce image quality, so you may need to balance prompt specificity with generation settings.  A practical starting setup is:  Prompt length: 2–4 sentences.  Lighting: one explicit source and one mood descriptor.  Camera: one shot type and one lens/depth cue.  Negative prompt: defects only, not style words.  Iterate by changing one variable at a time.

title: GPT-image 2 Production
content: It's a reasoning-powered model — it "thinks" before generating, which is why it handles dense text, infographics, UI mockups, and multi-panel compositions cleanly where older models produced garbled results. It supports up to 2K resolution natively and can generate up to 8 consistent images in a single prompt.  Prompting for Production/Visual Graphs For slides, diagrams, charts, and productivity visuals, OpenAI's official guide recommends treating your prompt like an artifact spec, not an illustration request. Key principles:  Name the exact deliverable: Say "pitch deck slide," "workflow diagram," or "production flow chart" explicitly — not just "make a chart"  Include real data/text inline: Paste actual numbers, labels, and axis names directly in the prompt  Use landscape sizing: 1536x864 for deck-style or widescreen outputs  Set quality="high": Required for small text, legends, and data labels  Quote literal text: Wrap any in-image text in quotes or ALL CAPS for accurate rendering  Example prompt structure for a production graph:  text Create a [pitch deck / production pipeline / Gantt chart] slide titled "[Title]". Use a clean white background, modern sans-serif typography. Include: - [specific data points, axis labels, values] - [legend, footnotes, company placeholder] Design should be highly readable, polished, professional startup-style visual language. No decorative elements, gradients, or shadows. quality="high" Prompt Structure Formula The official recommended order is:  Background/scene → Subject → Key details → Constraints → Intended use  For text-heavy production visuals specifically, use quality="high" and structure prompts with labeled line-breaks rather than one long paragraph — it makes debugging faster.  ComfyUI Integration: Yes, Fully Supported Yes, you can access gpt-image-2 directly in ComfyUI via Partner Nodes. That's a killer pipeline for Deep Vibe content. title: GPT-image 2 Img Creation
content: The Core Mental Model gpt-image-2 runs a reasoning pass before drawing — it interprets intent, not just keywords. This means you write prompts like a creative director briefing a photographer or illustrator, not a keyword list for a search engine. Give it the what, who it's for, what mood, and where it will be used — the model fills the craft gap itself.  The first ~50 words carry the most weight — front-load style, medium, and subject. Save secondary props and background accents for the end.  The Universal Prompt Template Use this as your default scaffold for every generation:  text Scene: [Where this happens — environment, time of day, background, location]  Subject: [Who or what is the main focus — be specific about age, clothing, texture, materials]  Important details: [Lighting source + quality, camera/lens feel, composition, depth, mood, surface textures]  Use case: [editorial photo / product mockup / brand ad / hero illustration / concept frame / storyboard]  Constraints: [no watermark / no logos / no extra text / preserve face / preserve layout / no cartoon style] Photorealistic Production Photography The Golden Rule Describe the photograph, not the fantasy. Think: lens, frame, time of day, light source, texture, surface wear, believable imperfection. If you want a photo, say "photo" — include the word photorealistic or substitute "real photograph", "taken on a real camera", "professional photography", or "shot on iPhone" depending on the intended aesthetic.  Lens + Camera Language These cinematic and photographic cues directly improve output quality:  "35mm film photography" → documentary/editorial feel  "shot on 85mm lens, f/1.4" → shallow DOF, portraiture  "medium format" → fashion/luxury editorial richness  "50mm lens, eye level" → neutral, natural perspective  "wide angle, low angle" → environmental, powerful, immersive  "macro detail" → product, texture, food, nature  "handheld, slight motion blur" → UGC/authentic street feel  Lighting Language Lighting Cue	Best For "Golden hour, warm side light"	Lifestyle, fashion, outdoor brand "Soft diffuse window light"	Beauty, editorial, interiors "Hard studio flash, high contrast"	Product, fashion, editorial bold "Overcast natural light, flat and even"	Clean product shots, lookbook "Practical neon, mixed color temperature"	Urban, nightlife, tech brand "Backlit silhouette, strong rim light"	Cinematic hero, drama, concept "Ring light, skin-forward glow"	Beauty, UGC, testimonial style Photorealism Negative Constraints Always append these when realism is the goal:  text No watermark. No logos. No stylized rendering. No cartoon elements. No heavy retouching. No artificial skin smoothing. No unnatural lens flare. Photography Template Examples Brand Lifestyle  text Photorealistic editorial photograph. Scene: a sun-drenched coastal café terrace at golden hour, Mediterranean architecture, warm stone walls. Subject: a woman in her early 30s, relaxed, wearing a cream linen dress, hands wrapped around an espresso cup. Soft side light from the left, shallow depth of field, background blurred with bokeh. Shot on 85mm lens, medium format feel. Mood: effortless luxury, quiet confidence. Use case: premium brand lifestyle ad. No text, no watermarks, no staged quality. Product Shot  text Photorealistic product photography. Scene: plain white opaque background, no environment. Subject: [product name] centered, clean silhouette, no halos or fringing. Lighting: soft diffuse studio light from camera-left, subtle contact shadow at base. Shot quality: sharp macro detail, high clarity. Preserve product geometry and label text exactly. No restyle. No extra elements. quality="high" Cinematic Portrait  text Cinematic portrait photograph. Scene: [environment]. Subject: [description — age, hair, clothing, expression]. Strong backlight with rim light outlining the figure, deep foreground shadow, minor lens flare from the light source. Shallow depth of field, 50mm lens, slight film grain. Mood: [adjective]. Style reference: Denis Villeneuve / Annie Leibovitz / Gregory Crewdson. Aspect ratio 16:9. Creative Illustrations Medium-First Approach State the visual medium explicitly at the top of the prompt — the model locks its entire rendering pipeline to that mode:  Medium Keyword	Output Style "oil painting"	Rich texture, visible brushwork, fine art "gouache illustration"	Flat opaque color, editorial/magazine "ink and watercolor"	Line art + wash, hand-made feel "3D render, Octane/Cinema4D"	Glossy, product/brand/motion graphics "cel animation style"	Clean fills, 2D animation look "risograph print"	Layered ink, indie/zine aesthetic "graphic novel panel"	Sequential art, high contrast line "vector flat illustration"	Clean shapes, icon/brand use "concept art, matte painting"	Film/game pre-production quality Illustration Texture & Quality Levers Add these sparingly to push production quality:  Photography analog: film grain, lens aberration, depth of field  Illustration analog: textured brushstrokes, visible paper grain, impasto texture, ink bleed  3D/render analog: subsurface scattering, ambient occlusion, ray-traced reflections  Universal: high detail, rich midtones, balanced composition  Illustration Templates Brand Illustration / Hero Art  text [Medium: e.g. "gouache editorial illustration"]. Scene: [environment description]. Subject: [character/object description]. Color palette: [3–4 hex-adjacent colors or palette name]. Lighting: [light direction + quality]. Composition: [framing]. Mood: [adjective]. Style influences: [e.g., "Malika Favre / Moebius / Studio Ghibli background art"]. Intended use: brand campaign hero image. Size: 1536x1024. quality="high". Multi-Panel Storyboard / Comic Reel  text Create a [4/6]-panel vertical comic strip for a [brand/story] campaign. Panel 1: [Scene description — action, framing, expression] Panel 2: [Beat 2] Panel 3: [Beat 3] Panel 4: [Resolution] Consistent character design across all panels. Clean gutters between panels. Style: [medium]. No dialogue bubbles unless specified. Size: 1024x1536. quality="medium". Concept Art / World-Building  text Matte painting concept art. Ultra-wide cinematic environment. Scene: [world description — biome, architecture, atmosphere, time of day]. No foreground characters. Atmospheric depth haze. Detailed mid-ground and background layers. Color mood: [warm/cool/split-tone]. Style: film concept art, [reference director or studio]. Aspect ratio: 16:9. quality="high". Advanced Production Techniques Character Consistency Across Multiple Frames Use a reference image and anchor all variations to it:  text Keep [character]'s facial features, hair, skin tone, and body type exactly the same as the reference image. Change only: [pose / expression / outfit / setting]. Maintain the same [photorealistic / illustration] style throughout. Do not copy the original subject — only the aesthetic DNA. Lighting & Scene Variants (for batch production) text Same image. Change only the time of day to [golden hour / blue hour / midday / overcast night]. Do not alter: subject, pose, composition, clothing, face, layout, any text. Match environmental lighting to the new time of day naturally. title: GPT-image 2 World Building
content: PURPOSE OF THIS CONTEXT This context teaches an LLM how to write prompts for gpt-image-2 specifically for world-building asset production: generating multi-angle views of locations, characters placed inside environments, and multi-character scenes — all driven by reference images (location reference + character sheets as inputs).  HOW GPT-IMAGE-2 PROCESSES MULTIPLE REFERENCE IMAGES gpt-image-2 accepts up to 14 input images in a single call. When multiple images are passed, the LLM prompt must:  Label each input by index and role: "Image 1: location reference. Image 2: character sheet for [Name]. Image 3: character sheet for [Name 2]."  Explicitly describe how they interact: "Place the character from Image 2 inside the environment from Image 1"  Never assume the model infers relationships — state every compositional relationship explicitly  The model reads the prompt first, then cross-references the input images against it. Front-load all identity and location preservation rules — they carry the most weight.  CORE PROMPT STRUCTURE FOR WORLD-BUILDING Always write prompts in this exact section order:  text INPUT LABELING      → Identify each reference image by index and role LOCATION            → Preserve or expand the environment CHARACTER(S)        → Lock character identity from sheet SHOT / ANGLE        → Specify camera angle, framing, distance SCENE ACTION        → Describe what is happening in the frame LIGHTING            → Match, shift, or define lighting for this shot STYLE               → Photorealistic / illustrated / cinematic — must match reference aesthetic OUTPUT INTENT       → What this asset is for (key art / storyboard / environment sheet / turnaround) PRESERVE LIST       → Explicit list of everything that must NOT change LOCATION / ENVIRONMENT RULES Preserving the Location Reference When an environment reference image is provided:  text Image 1 is the location reference. Preserve all architectural structures, spatial layout,  color palette, time of day, atmospheric conditions, and surface materials from Image 1 exactly. Do not redesign, simplify, or reinterpret the environment. Only change: [what you want changed]. Generating New Angles from a Location Reference For world-building, you need the same location from multiple camera positions:  text Image 1 is the location reference. Generate this same location from a [new angle]: - "wide establishing shot from street level, slightly low angle" - "interior looking outward through the main entrance" - "overhead bird's-eye view, top-down" - "close-up architectural detail — [specific element]" - "same scene, camera positioned 90 degrees to the left of the original view" Preserve all visual design, materials, lighting mood, and color palette from Image 1 exactly. Only the camera angle and framing changes. Environment Expansion To expand the world beyond the reference frame:  text Image 1 shows one section of this location. Extend the environment to the [left / right / background / underground]. Match all architectural style, color palette, materials, and atmospheric lighting from Image 1 exactly. New areas should feel like they are part of the same world — consistent design language throughout. Lighting/Time Variants of the Same Location text Image 1 is the location reference. Generate the same location at [golden hour / blue hour /  overcast midday / rainy night / interior candlelight].  Match all spatial layout and architecture exactly. Change only: the time-of-day lighting, sky, and atmospheric conditions. Do not alter: structure, materials, color relationships, any design elements. CHARACTER SHEET RULES How to Reference a Character Sheet Always specify what to extract and what to lock:  text Image [X] is the character sheet for [NAME].  Use this sheet to lock the following and never alter them: - Face: facial structure, eye shape and color, nose, lips, jawline - Hair: color, length, texture, style - Skin: tone, any markings, freckles, scars - Body: proportions, height relative to environment, build - Costume/outfit: every garment, accessory, color, and material - Any distinguishing features: [list specifics]  This character's identity is fixed. Do not redesign, reinterpret, or smooth any features. Character Sheet to Scene Placement text Image 1: location reference. Image 2: character sheet for [NAME]. Place [NAME] from Image 2 into the environment from Image 1. Position: [left-center / foreground / mid-ground / behind the main structure]. Pose: [standing relaxed / walking toward camera / seated / looking away]. Scale: character should appear [natural human scale / small against the environment]. Lighting on character: match the environment light source from Image 1 —  add a subtle rim light from [direction] to separate character from background. Preserve all character identity from Image 2. Do not alter face, outfit, or proportions. SHOT TYPE VOCABULARY Use these exact framing descriptors in every world-building prompt:  Shot Name	Description	Best Used For Extreme wide / establishing	Full environment, character small or absent	Location reveals, world scale Wide shot	Character fully visible, environment dominant	Character-in-world placement Medium shot	Character waist-up, environment visible	Character + location context Medium close-up	Character chest-up	Emotion + environment behind Close-up	Face and shoulders	Character emotion, detail sheet Over-the-shoulder	Behind one character, facing another	Dialogue, multi-character Low angle	Camera below subject, looking up	Power, scale, drama High angle / bird's eye	Camera above, looking down	Location layout, overhead map Dutch angle	Camera tilted ~15-20 degrees	Tension, instability POV shot	First-person perspective from character	Immersion, environment walkthrough Profile / 90-degree	Character viewed from the side	Character turnaround, silhouette MULTI-CHARACTER SCENE RULES When placing 2+ characters from different character sheets into a scene:  text Image 1: location reference. Image 2: character sheet for [CHARACTER A — NAME]. Image 3: character sheet for [CHARACTER B — NAME].  Place [CHARACTER A] and [CHARACTER B] together inside the environment from Image 1. [CHARACTER A] is positioned [foreground left / right / center]. [CHARACTER B] is positioned [background / facing A / beside A]. Interaction: [describe — facing each other / walking side by side / one looking at the other]. Framing: [wide two-shot / over-the-shoulder on A / medium group shot]. Lighting: match Image 1's environment light. Both characters lit consistently with the scene.  CRITICAL: Do not merge, blend, or compromise either character's identity. [CHARACTER A]: preserve all features from Image 2 exactly. [CHARACTER B]: preserve all features from Image 3 exactly. They must be visually distinct and individually identifiable. CHARACTER TURNAROUND SHEETS For generating multiple angles of the same character from their sheet:  text Image 1 is the character sheet for [NAME]. Generate a character turnaround panel showing [NAME] from four angles in a single image: - Front view (0°) - 3/4 view (45°)   - Profile / side view (90°) - Back view (180°) All four views on a plain white / neutral background. Character stands in a neutral T-pose or relaxed standing pose. Consistent costume, proportions, and identity across all four angles. Same lighting (flat soft diffuse studio light) on all views. No background elements. No shadow below. Clean character sheet format. Preserve all features from Image 1 exactly across every angle. ASSET TYPE TEMPLATES Environment Establishing Shot (No Characters) text INPUT: Image 1 — location reference TASK: Generate an ultra-wide establishing shot of this location. Preserve all architectural design, spatial layout, color palette, and atmosphere from Image 1. Camera: extreme wide angle, low horizon, slightly elevated viewpoint. Show the full scope and scale of the environment. Atmospheric depth: add subtle haze for depth and distance. Lighting: [match Image 1 / shift to: golden hour / night / overcast]. Style: [cinematic photorealism / matte painting concept art / illustrated]. Size: 2560x1440. quality="high". PRESERVE: All environmental design from Image 1. Do not add characters. Character Hero Shot in Location text INPUT: Image 1 — location. Image 2 — character sheet for [NAME]. TASK: Generate a hero-framing shot of [NAME] inside this environment. Camera: medium shot, [eye-level / slight low angle], [NAME] positioned center-frame. [NAME] is [action/pose]. Expression: [specific]. Lighting: match Image 1's environment. Add rim light from [direction]. Style: [cinematic photorealism / illustrated]. Size: 1536x1024. quality="high". PRESERVE: Character identity from Image 2 — face, hair, outfit, proportions. PRESERVE: Environment design from Image 1 — architecture, palette, atmosphere. Location Angle Exploration Pack (n=4) text INPUT: Image 1 — location reference. TASK: Generate 4 different camera angles of this same location. Each image shows the same environment from a distinct angle: n=1: Wide establishing — front-facing, eye level n=2: Interior looking outward through the main entrance n=3: High angle / bird's eye — overhead looking down n=4: Ground level close-up of a key architectural detail  Preserve all visual design, materials, and color palette from Image 1 across all 4 frames. n=4. Size: 1536x1024. quality="medium". Storyboard Beat Panel text INPUT: Image 1 — location. Image 2 — character sheet for [NAME]. TASK: Generate storyboard panel [#X] of [total]. SCENE BEAT: [Describe exactly what is happening in this moment of the story]. Camera: [shot type + angle]. Action: [NAME] is [specific action — not vague]. Emotional beat: [what the audience should feel]. Style: [cinematic / illustrated / graphic novel]. Size: 1024x1536. quality="medium". PRESERVE: Character identity. Environment design. Consistent visual style across panels. WORLD-BUILDING SETTINGS REFERENCE text Environment establishing / concept art:   quality="high",   size="2560x1440" Character hero shot in location:          quality="high",   size="1536x1024" Portrait / vertical character shot:       quality="high",   size="1024x1536" Character turnaround sheet:               quality="high",   size="1536x1024" Storyboard panels:                        quality="medium", size="1024x1536", n=4-6 Angle exploration pack:                   quality="medium", size="1536x1024", n=4 Rapid concept variants:                   quality="low",    size="1536x1024", n=8 CRITICAL RULES — NEVER BREAK THESE These are the highest-priority rules from OpenAI's official guide and production testing:  Always label inputs by index — "Image 1 is X. Image 2 is Y." Never assume the model knows which is which  Say "exactly" and "identical to" — never "inspired by" or "based on" — those permit drift  Lock face and costume separately — they drift independently; preserve both explicitly every prompt  End every prompt with a PRESERVE list — list every element that must survive the generation  Never overload one prompt — if the scene is complex, run a quality="low" n=8 draft pass first, pick the best composition, then run quality="high" on the winner  Re-specify invariants on every iteration — the model has no persistent memory across calls; repeat all identity locks every time  Describe body scale explicitly — "character appears at natural human scale relative to the architecture" prevents giant/tiny character errors  State distinct identity for multi-character — "CHARACTER A and CHARACTER B must be visually distinct and individually identifiable" prevents face-merging

title: Fibo
content:
# Fibo — Structured-JSON Image Generation (spatial control)

## Use when
Deterministic spatial composition through structured JSON: storyboard keyframes where character staging must be exact, multi-character scenes where left/center/right positioning matters, base-composition passes that will be refined downstream (inpaint, LoRA reskin), repeatable layouts across an episode where the same JSON shape drives many frames.

## Prompt skeleton (structured_prompt JSON payload)
```json
{
  "objects": [
    {
      "id": "____",
      "character_asset": "____",
      "location": "left | center | right",
      "relative_size": "small | medium | large",
      "action": "[one concrete verb phrase — what the body is doing in this single frame]",
      "expression": "AU__+AU__ [from FACS Reference]",
      "pose": "[body orientation]",
      "relationship": "[inter-character dynamic]"
    }
  ],
  "background_setting": "____ [environment, props, atmosphere]",
  "lighting": {
    "style": "____ [from Lighting Vocabulary Reference]",
    "direction": "____",
    "shadows": "____"
  },
  "camera": {
    "angle": "____ [from Camera Grammar Reference]",
    "framing": "____",
    "depth_of_field": "____",
    "feel": "____"
  },
  "aesthetics": {
    "color_scheme": "____",
    "aesthetic_score": "very high",
    "preference_score": "very high"
  },
  "artistic_style": "____",
  "style_medium": "____"
}
```

## Caps (exceed -> ambiguous output, averaged expressions)
- <= 3 distinct objects (characters or major props) per scene before staging clarity drops.
- ONE concrete verb phrase per `action` field — vague strings produce ambiguous poses.
- <= 2-3 FACS units per character's `expression` field — more averages into neutral.
- `aesthetic_score` and `preference_score` always set to `"very high"` to push polish.
- Set explicit `image_size.width` and `image_size.height` — Fibo defaults to square.

## Input contract
- Every `objects[]` entry needs `id` (stable handle matching your asset registry) + `character_asset` (downstream LoRA name or reference image label).
- `location` is a controlled vocab: left / center / right ONLY — this is the layout-deterministic field.
- `relative_size` is small / medium / large — controls visual hierarchy.

## Pull concrete vocab (mandatory — Fibo rewards specificity)
- `expression` → FACS Reference AU codes (e.g., `"AU6+AU12 genuine smile"`).
- `camera` block (angle / framing / depth_of_field / feel) → Camera Grammar Reference terms.
- `lighting` block (style / direction / shadows) → Lighting Vocabulary Reference (named patterns, direction codes, Kelvin temperatures).

## Negatives
Fibo's structured input largely eliminates the need for natural-language negatives — the JSON already constrains the scene. If using a parallel text prompt field, keep negatives short: "no identity drift, no extra characters, no background substitution, no AI-generated look."

## Bookend (restate at end of any natural-language wrapper around the JSON)
"All staging follows the structured_prompt exactly. Character identity is approximate — downstream identity-lock pass required."

## Practical default
Define every character in `objects[]` with explicit `location` and `relative_size`. Lock `aesthetics` scores to `"very high"`. Keep `action` to one concrete verb per character. Pull all camera/lighting/expression terms from the reference rows. Pair every Fibo run with a downstream identity-lock pass (Qwen Image Edit 2511 i2i + character LoRA, or Nano Banana 2/Pro World Building with reference images).

---
## Why this context (rationale)
Fibo's structured_prompt is the only image-gen API that gives you positional certainty — diffusion models with natural-language prompts can't reliably stage left/center/right. Output is compositionally accurate but character identity is approximate. The workflow: Fibo for layout-deterministic base keyframes → downstream identity-locked pass for face/character fidelity. Use it for storyboard production and any multi-character scene where staging matters more than identity at the base-frame stage.

content: Example Prompt: Style: Hybrid visual style — photorealistic, documentary-level environment combined with stylized 3D animated characters. The subject and the fan are fully 3D animated characters seamlessly composited into a live-action realistic world. Single continuous unbroken shot from a handheld camera within a dense crowd. Natural micro-shake, eye-level perspective.  Character Style: The subject from @Image1 is rendered as a polished 3D animated character with stylized proportions, soft subsurface skin shading, expressive features, and clean rim lighting — while maintaining a perfectly consistent face and the exact outfit from the reference image. The fan they interact with is also a 3D animated character in the same rendering style. Both characters retain cinematic CG quality with realistic interaction with the surrounding light (flash bounces, streetlight highlights, shadow casting on real ground). Mixed reflections on polished surfaces (phones, cars), soft realistic shadows, and a slight atmospheric haze for depth. The crowd, barricades, hotel facade, SUVs, and street are all live-action realistic — only the two main characters are stylized 3D.  Subject: The 3D animated subject maintains a calm, controlled presence with a subtle, confident smile, perfectly matching the face and outfit from @Image1. As the camera lifts slightly above shoulder level, the 3D animated subject exits a luxury hotel in the background. Bright media flashes erupt, illuminating the CG character against the realistic environment. Real security personnel step into frame, pushing the crowd back, causing the camera to shake naturally. Through shifting gaps in the crowd, the animated subject walks forward clearly into center frame. The camera pans to follow as a luxury convoy of three premium black SUVs (photorealistic) pulls up. A real security guard opens the back door of the middle SUV. The animated subject steps inside, rolls down the window to wave one last time, and the vehicles begin to pull away as the realistic crowd jumps to capture the moment.  Audio: Loud, chaotic crowd cheering and whistling. Overlapping voices shouting the subject's name. A barrage of rapid camera shutter clicks. Distant New York City sirens and traffic.
