title: Seedance v2.0 Reference Styleframes
content: Generic Seedance 2.0 “Continuous Storyboard” Prompt Use this as your base template; anything in <angleBrackets> is a variable your system fills from the styleframe sheet / production doc.  Transform this 2x2 storyboard grid into a single fluid cinematic sequence. Generate one continuous, unbroken shot that moves through four distinct narrative beats, following the natural reading order from left‑to‑right, top‑to‑bottom. The video must feel like a single take, not four separate clips.  Use the uploaded storyboard sheet as the primary visual layout reference: @storyboard. Treat each panel as a keyframe you are moving through with the camera, not as separate shots to cut between.  Maintain strict character and design continuity across the entire sequence. All characters must keep the same body proportions, facial geometry, hairstyle, skin tone, wardrobe, and accessories as defined in the reference materials: @character_sheet (and any additional references such as @outfit_sheet, @prop_sheet). No morphing, no outfit changes, no age or body drift between beats. It must look like the same actor in the same outfit from first frame to last.  The camera should create seamless transitions between panels through motivated movement: follow character motion, dolly, pan, track, crane, or orbit to reveal the next beat. Do not hard‑cut between panels. Every change in framing must be justified by either character action or deliberate camera choreography.  Preserve all production design established in the storyboard and location description: environment layout, props, lighting direction, time of day, weather, and atmosphere should remain continuous unless explicitly stated otherwise in a beat. No random teleporting, no unexplained changes of environment or lighting.  Global production parameters Location (applies to all beats): <env>  Style / look: <stylePack>  Tone and mood: <toneKeywords>  Aspect ratio: 16:9 widescreen, full‑frame, no black bars.  Overall duration: <totalDurationSeconds> seconds, evenly distributing time across the four beats unless otherwise specified.  Audio: Use the uploaded voice‑over track @voice_over as the primary audio. Sync character performance, pacing, and camera movement to the rhythm, emphasis, and timing of the VO. No additional music unless specified. Keep sound design minimal and natural (subtle diegetic ambience matching the environment).  Beat‑by‑beat structure (reading order) Treat the following as a mini‑timeline inside one continuous shot. Timecodes are approximate anchors within <totalDurationSeconds>:  Beat 1 (0s–~25% of total duration) Use the first panel of the storyboard as the starting framing reference.  Visual focus: <beat1_visual>  Character action and blocking: <beat1_action>  Camera: <beat1_camera> (e.g., static wide, slow push‑in, tracking from left to right)  Emotional tone: <beat1_emotion> The opening frame should closely match the composition of panel 1 in @storyboard, then begin moving as described.  Transition 1 → 2 From Beat 1 into Beat 2, transition purely by camera and/or character movement, not a cut. Examples: continue the dolly, follow the character walking, or pan/tilt to reveal the next area of the environment that corresponds to panel 2.  Beat 2 (~25%–~50%) Use panel 2 as the keyframe reference for the new framing.  Visual focus: <beat2_visual>  Character action and blocking: <beat2_action>  Camera: <beat2_camera>  Emotional tone: <beat2_emotion> Ensure the entry pose and environment logically follow from the exit of Beat 1.  Transition 2 → 3 Again, no cut. Move the camera or let the character’s motion guide us toward the composition that matches panel 3, keeping lighting and environment consistent.  Beat 3 (~50%–~75%)  Visual focus: <beat3_visual>  Character action and blocking: <beat3_action>  Camera: <beat3_camera>  Emotional tone: <beat3_emotion> Use panel 3 of @storyboard as your target composition, then let the shot evolve through the described motion.  Transition 3 → 4 Continue the same approach: use camera choreography and character motion to naturally arrive at the panel‑4 composition, without cutting.  Beat 4 (~75%–100%)  Visual focus: <beat4_visual>  Character action and blocking: <beat4_action>  Camera: <beat4_camera>  Emotional tone: <beat4_emotion> Land on a strong closing composition inspired by panel 4, holding or resolving the action in a way that fits the VO ending and the overall tone. Optionally, use a subtle move like a slow pull‑back or push‑in to close.  Character and environment continuity rules Characters: Keep identity locked to @character_sheet/@outfit_sheet definitions—no changes in facial structure, clothing, hair length/style, or body type across the entire clip.  Environment: Use the same location setup <env> across all beats unless a deliberate change is specified. The spatial layout should feel consistent when the camera moves.  Lighting: Maintain one coherent lighting scenario (direction, color, intensity) matching the style and time of day, with only subtle local variations (e.g., character moving through light pools).  Camera and motion directives Throughout the sequence:  Prioritize smooth, physically plausible camera movement (tracking, dolly, pan, tilt, crane, orbit) over jumpy or teleporting framing changes.  Make sure character motion, props, and environment react consistently (e.g., footsteps, cloth, hair, particles) to the camera’s movement and the environment.  The aesthetic should feel like grounded, documentary‑style professional cinematography rather than hyper‑stylized cuts between still images.  Director notes and constraints Director notes: <directorNotes> (additional nuance on pacing, emotional beats, or micro‑blocking).  Respect all storyboard compositions, but interpret them as moments within a single evolving shot, not rigid frozen frames.  No on‑screen text, no captions, no subtitles, and no UI overlays of any kind.  Do not add logos, watermarks, or title cards.  Do not introduce new characters, props, or locations beyond what is defined in <env>, the storyboard, and the reference sheets.

title: Seedream 4.5
content: Use this structure every time:  Base formula  Reference role: “Use reference image 1 as the character anchor and reference image 2 as the location anchor.”  Identity lock: “Preserve facial features, hairstyle, body proportions, and signature clothing details.”  Location lock: “Preserve architecture, layout, perspective, and key landmarks.”  Scene change: “Generate [new action/story beat] in [new mood/time/weather].”  Camera direction: “Compose as [close-up / medium shot / wide shot / full-body], from [angle].”  Quality direction: “Cinematic lighting, realistic materials, coherent shadows, consistent spatial depth.”  That gives the model clear hierarchy: who, where, what changes, and what stays fixed.  Reusable templates 1) Standard narrative scene “Use reference image 1 as the main character anchor and reference image 2 as the location anchor. Keep the character’s facial features, hairstyle, proportions, and overall identity consistent. Preserve the location’s architecture, layout, and recognizable visual landmarks. Generate a scene where the character is [action] inside [location], with [lighting], [weather/time of day], and a [mood] atmosphere. Frame it as a [shot type] with natural perspective and cinematic realism.”  2) Cinematic story beat “Using the character from reference image 1 and the location from reference image 2, create a cinematic still of [moment]. Keep the same character identity and preserve the location’s spatial continuity. Change only the [expression/pose/wardrobe/lighting/weather] to match the story. Use dramatic composition, strong depth, and film-like lighting.”  3) Emotional portrait in place “Keep the character from reference image 1 exactly recognizable, and keep the environment from reference image 2 intact. Place the character in [location] and show [emotion] through expression and posture. Use a [close-up / waist-up] composition, soft directional light, and subtle environmental detail to reinforce the mood.”  4) Action scene in a known place “Use reference image 1 for the character and reference image 2 for the location. Preserve character identity, outfit details, and the exact location layout. Show the character [running / turning / talking / arriving / observing] in the scene, with motion cues, realistic shadows, and a dynamic camera angle.”  5) Before-and-after variant “Keep the same character and location references, but transform the scene into [time of day / season / weather / event]. Maintain continuity in face, architecture, and composition while changing the atmosphere to feel like a different moment in the same story.”  Fill-in library Use these as modular blocks you can paste into templates.  Character identity blocks “Preserve facial features, hairstyle, skin tone, age range, and body proportions.”  “Keep the same signature outfit unless otherwise specified.”  “Maintain the character’s recognizable expression and design language.”  “Do not redesign the face or alter the character’s identity.”  Location continuity blocks “Preserve the building geometry, room layout, and key landmarks.”  “Keep the same street composition, signage, and environmental structure.”  “Maintain the interior architecture and spatial arrangement.”  “Use the reference location as the exact setting, not just inspiration.”  Scene change blocks “Change the character’s pose from static to walking.”  “Change the expression from neutral to tense.”  “Change the weather to rain.”  “Change the time of day to sunset.”  “Add subtle environmental motion such as wind, reflections, or crowd flow.”  Camera and composition blocks “Compose as a wide establishing shot.”  “Compose as a medium shot with the character centered in frame.”  “Compose as a close-up portrait with shallow depth of field.”  “Use a low-angle cinematic perspective.”  “Keep the location readable in the background.”  Lighting and mood blocks “Use soft natural daylight.”  “Use dramatic side lighting with strong contrast.”  “Use moody blue ambient light.”  “Use warm golden-hour lighting.”  “Create a suspenseful, quiet, cinematic atmosphere.”  Prompt library by use case Story continuity “Use reference image 1 for the character and reference image 2 for the location. Keep both fully recognizable. Generate the next scene in the story, showing [action] after [previous event]. Maintain visual continuity, realistic lighting, and coherent environment details.”  Character in different locations “Keep the same character identity from reference image 1. Place them into the location from reference image 2 and preserve the location’s architectural logic and landmarks. Make the scene feel like the character naturally belongs there.”  Location with different characters “Use reference image 2 as the exact location anchor. Replace the original subject with the character from reference image 1 while preserving spatial continuity and environmental detail.”  Editorial-style still “Using the character and location references, create a polished editorial image of [subject/action]. Keep the identity and setting consistent, with refined composition, clean lighting, and a believable real-world atmosphere.”  Prompt formula cheat sheet You can think of each prompt as:  Anchor + Lock + Change + Frame + Light + Mood  Example: “Use reference image 1 as the character anchor and reference image 2 as the location anchor. Lock the identity, outfit, architecture, and spatial layout. Change the scene to a rainy evening arrival. Frame it as a wide cinematic shot with wet reflections and a tense, moody atmosphere.”  Production tips Repeat the same identity words every time if you want consistency across a batch.  Be explicit about what should not change; the model responds better when constraints are named.  If the character is primary, mention them first. If the location is primary, mention the environment first.  Keep scene changes limited to one or two variables per prompt for cleaner results.  For multi-image sequences, keep a stable base phrase and only swap the action line.  Copy-paste master template “Use reference image 1 as the character anchor and reference image 2 as the location anchor. Preserve the character’s facial features, hairstyle, proportions, and recognizable outfit details. Preserve the location’s architecture, layout, perspective, and key landmarks. Generate a scene of [action] with [lighting], [weather/time of day], and a [mood] atmosphere. Compose it as a [shot type] from [camera angle], with cinematic realism and strong spatial continuity.”

title: Nano Banana 2 Production
content:
# Nano Banana 2 — Production Graphics (slides, charts, diagrams, infographics, text-in-image)

## Use when
Editable production assets where typography and dense layout must read cleanly: pitch decks, slide titles, charts, workflow diagrams, infographics, packaging mocks, brand visualizations.

## Prompt skeleton
```
Create a [pitch deck slide / workflow diagram / Gantt chart / two-column infographic] titled "____".
Title reads "____". Subhead reads "____". Body reads "____", "____", "____". Footer reads "____".
Background: ____. Typography: ____ sans-serif, ____ weight, ____ color.
Layout: ____ (16:9 / 4:5 / 1:1). Grid: 12-column. Hierarchy: title 3x body, generous whitespace.
```

## Caps (exceed -> label crowding, garbled text)
- <= 4 distinct text blocks per image.
- <= 30 words per body block — split or summarize beyond that.
- <= 6 labeled regions per infographic.
- <= 2 typography hierarchy levels per artifact (title + body, or title + subhead + body).

## Negatives
No decorative flourishes, no gradients, no drop shadows, no extra unspecified text, no watermark, no logo, no busy background, no photographic textures, no AI-generated look, no clip-art aesthetic.

## Pull concrete vocab
- Layout / grid / hierarchy → Camera Grammar Reference (composition terms only).
- Any photo elements inside the layout (e.g., portrait inside a slide) → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Every text block rendered exactly as quoted. No extra text. No decorative additions."

## Practical default
Quote every literal text block. Front-load the artifact type. Cap at 4 text blocks. Thinking level High for any chart with >4 data points. 2K for proofs, 4K for final.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
NB2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) runs a brief reasoning pass before drawing, which is why it handles dense text, infographics, and UI mockups cleanly where older Flash-class models garbled words. Use Pro variant when the artifact must hold up at print/billboard grade; use NB2 here for fast iteration and production-grade output on standard slide/diagram surfaces.

title: Nano Banana 2 Img Creation
content:
# Nano Banana 2 — Image Creation (photoreal + illustration)

## Use when
Single-image photoreal or illustration outputs: brand lifestyle shots, product photography, editorial portraits, hero key art, social assets, concept frames. Faster and cheaper than Pro; trade is slightly less headroom on dense complexity.

## Prompt skeleton
```
[STYLE ANCHOR — "photorealistic photograph" or explicit medium] of [SUBJECT + DETAILS],
[ACTION] in [ENVIRONMENT], [COMPOSITION + CAMERA + LENS],
[LIGHTING + DIRECTION + TEMPERATURE], [STYLE INFLUENCE], [USE CASE].
```

## Caps (exceed -> mode bleed, plastic output)
- ONE style mode per prompt — photoreal OR illustration, never both ("photo … but illustrated" produces muddy hybrids).
- <= 80 words per prompt; <= 40 for product-style clarity work.
- <= 2 named style influences; one dominant, one secondary.
- <= 3 facial expression cues per subject (see FACS).

## Negatives
No waxy skin, no over-smoothed face, no plastic look, no extra fingers, no warped faces, no AI-generated look, no watermark, no logos, no stylized rendering when photoreal is the goal, no photographic textures when illustration is the goal.

## Pull concrete vocab
- Shot type, angle, lens, depth of field → Camera Grammar Reference.
- Light direction, quality, temperature, source, named patterns → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.
- Any facial expression → FACS Reference AU codes.

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Photoreal mode locked: natural skin texture, no AI-look, no plastic." (or: "Illustration mode locked: [medium] technique, [palette], no photographic bleed-through.")

## Practical default
Photoreal: 85mm at f/2.8, named directional light, era+medium style anchor, FACS expression, mitigation negatives on for faces. Illustration: explicit medium at front, palette + texture cues, commit to one style.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
NB2 handles photoreal and illustration cleanly when you commit fully to one mode at the start of the prompt — the model treats the first ~50 words as the dominant style signal. Pro variant outperforms on premium/print-grade work; use NB2 here for fast iteration and standard publication-grade output.

title: Nano Banana 2 World Building
content:
# Nano Banana 2 — World Building (multi-image fusion)

## Use when
Multi-reference composition where character + location + wardrobe need to fuse coherently: character-in-location, multi-character scenes, environment expansion, character turnarounds, brand-sheet composites. Lighter-weight than Pro — use this for standard production; reach for Pro when reference count is high or print-grade fidelity matters.

## Prompt skeleton
Index every input, then give ONE composition delta:
```
Image 1: location (full environment).
Image 2: character sheet for [NAME].
Image 3: wardrobe for [NAME] (optional).

Place [NAME] (Image 2, wearing Image 3) in the environment from Image 1, [position], [pose + shot type — Camera Grammar term].
```

## Preserve / change (exhaustive)
```
Preserve Image 1: architecture, materials, palette, lighting direction, time of day.
Preserve Image 2: facial structure, eye shape+color, hairstyle, skin tone, proportions.
Preserve Image 3: every garment, accessory, color, material, fit.
Change only: the pose + interaction in the action line.
```

## Caps (exceed -> identity merge, drift)
- <= 4 references per call (NB2 starts dropping fidelity past 4).
- <= 2 distinct characters before identity-merge risk climbs.
- Exactly ONE composition delta per generation.
- Turnaround: <= 4 views in one image.

## Distinct-identity (multi-character — mandatory)
```
Critical: [NAME A] and [NAME B] must be visually distinct and individually identifiable. Do not merge, blend, or average identities. [NAME A]: preserve Image 2 features exactly. [NAME B]: preserve Image 3 features exactly.
```

## Scale + lighting match (always both)
- Scale: state subject occupancy (e.g., "~40% frame height, natural human scale relative to architecture").
- Lighting: "lit by the same [Lighting Vocab term] as Image 1 — match shadow geometry, warmth, contrast."

## Pull concrete vocab
- Framing / angle / shot → Camera Grammar Reference.
- Light direction / quality / temperature → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.
- Facial expression → FACS Reference AU codes.

## Negatives
No identity merge, no feature drift, no environment palette/material drift, no lighting mismatch, no scale errors, no extra unrequested characters, no wardrobe invention, no background substitution, no AI-generated look.

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Identity locked per Image 2 and environment preserved per Image 1 — exactly."

## Practical default
Index inputs → exhaustive preserve list → ONE delta → scale + lighting match → distinct-identity (multi-char) → negatives → bookend the lock. Thinking level High. 2K.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
NB2 supports multi-image fusion at standard production grade; cap at 4 refs and 2 distinct characters is the practical sweet spot before identity drift compounds. Reach for Pro variant when reference count is higher or character count exceeds 2.

title: Nano Banana 2 Identity & Edits
content:
# Nano Banana 2 — Identity-Locked Edits

## Use when
Targeted edits where the source image's identity, composition, or structure must survive: background swaps with face lock, color/material changes, prop add/remove, style migration, time-of-day variants, wardrobe swaps, product recolor.

## Prompt skeleton (Keep + Change + How + Constraints)
```
Keep: [exhaustive list — face, pose, expression, clothing, hair, framing, branding, original key light direction].
Change: [single delta].
How: [technique + intensity + lighting handling].
Constraints: [explicit guardrails].
```

## Caps (exceed -> drift across edit dimensions)
- ONE composition delta per call.
- <= 3 preservation dimensions stated as "exact" (face, costume, branding usually).
- <= 2 lighting changes per call.
- Repeat the full block on every iteration — no persistent memory across calls.

## Preserve / change (exhaustive — list everything)
- **Face lock**: "Keep face: exact eye shape, jawline, nose, lips, skin tone, micro-features."
- **Costume lock**: "Keep costume: exact garments, accessory geometry, material drape, color, fit."
- **Brand lock**: "Keep all logos, typography, brand colors, text exactly as in source."
- **Composition lock**: "Keep exact framing, crop, subject scale, depth-of-field."

## Negatives
No facial drift, no wardrobe change unless specified, no recomposition, no logo or text mutation, no original background bleed-through, no double exposure, no ghost limbs, no JPEG artifacts from source, no chromatic aberration carryover.

## Pull concrete vocab
- Light direction match when re-lighting → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.
- Any expression change → FACS Reference AU codes.
- New framing if recomposing → Camera Grammar Reference.

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Face, pose, composition, and branding locked from source — only the change line applies. No drift on anything else."

## Practical default
Four-block structure every time. Keep list is exhaustive. Change is one delta. How names the technique. Constraints are explicit guardrails. Repeat in full on every iteration.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
NB2 has no persistent memory across calls — that's why the four-block structure must repeat in full per iteration. Lock face and costume separately even when they sound redundant; they drift independently.

Keep: subject's face, hair, expression, wardrobe, pose, framing, key light direction. Change: background to ____. How: photorealistic, match original key light from ____ [Lighting Vocab], add subtle rim from ____. Constraints: no facial drift, no wardrobe change, no recomposition. content:
# Nano Banana Pro — World Building (multi-image fusion)

## Use when
Composing character + location + wardrobe + prop references into one coherent scene: character-in-location, multi-character groups, turnarounds with secondary anchors, environment expansion, brand-sheet composites.

## Prompt skeleton
Index every input, then give ONE composition delta:
```
Image 1: location (full environment).
Image 2: character sheet for [NAME A].
Image 3: character sheet for [NAME B].
Image 4: wardrobe for [NAME A]. Image 5: prop — [name + use].

Place [NAME A] (Image 2, wearing Image 4) in the environment from Image 1, foreground-left. Place [NAME B] (Image 3) mid-ground-right. [NAME A] holds the prop from Image 5 in the right hand.
```

## Preserve / change (exhaustive)
```
Preserve Image 1: architecture, materials, palette, lighting direction, time of day, haze.
Preserve Image 2/3: facial structure, eye shape+color, hairstyle, skin tone, proportions.
Preserve Image 4: every garment, accessory, color, material, fit.
Preserve Image 5: prop geometry, material, color, label text.
Change only: the pose + interaction in the action line.
```

## Caps (exceed -> quality collapses)
- <= 5-6 references per call; <= 3 distinct characters before identity-merge risk climbs.
- Exactly ONE composition delta per generation. Multiple changes -> drift.
- Turnaround: <= 4 views in one image.
- Scale: state the subject's frame occupancy (e.g. "~35% frame height, natural human scale").

## Distinct-identity (multi-character — mandatory)
```
Critical: [NAME A] and [NAME B] must be visually distinct and individually identifiable. Do not merge, blend, or average identities. [NAME A]: preserve all Image 2 features exactly. [NAME B]: preserve all Image 3 features exactly.
```

## Scale + lighting match (always both)
- Scale: subject occupancy + human scale relative to architecture.
- Lighting: "lit by the same [window light, camera-right] as Image 1 — match shadow geometry, warmth, contrast."

## Pull concrete vocab (don't write abstract words)
- Framing/angle/shot -> use Camera Grammar Reference terms, not "dynamic angle."
- Light direction/quality/temperature -> use Lighting Vocabulary Reference, not "dramatic lighting."
- Any facial expression -> use FACS Reference AU codes, not "happy/serious."

## Negatives
No identity merge or blending, no feature drift, no environment palette/material drift, no lighting or shadow mismatch, no scale errors, no extra unrequested characters, no wardrobe/prop invention, no background substitution, no AI-generated look.

## Bookend (restate at the END of the emitted prompt)
Close every prompt by repeating the single hard constraint: "Identity locked per Image 2/3 and environment preserved per Image 1 — exactly."

## Practical default
Index inputs -> exhaustive preserve list -> ONE composition delta -> scale+lighting match -> distinct-identity language -> negatives -> bookend the lock. Thinking level High. 2K proofs, 4K final.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
Pro holds more references at higher fidelity than Flash 2, so it can carry a long preservation list without losing focus — that headroom is the whole reason to use it for multi-element scenes. Use-case shapes: brand hero (talent+wardrobe+location+prop, 4:5, 4K) | editorial group (5+ refs, 3:2, distinct-ID) | turnaround pack (1 ref, 4 angles, 21:9) | storyboard sequence (character+location held constant, vary action+camera per panel).

# Nano Banana Pro — Identity-Locked Edits (premium-grade)

Four-block structure every time. Triple-lock when brand chrome is in frame. Thinking level High for any edit with >2 preservation dimensions. 2K minimum, 4K for catalog/print.

Pro holds three independent identity dimensions (face, costume, brand) simultaneously without merging — the practical strength behind the premium price. Use this context whenever brand-chrome preservation is non-negotiable (catalog, OOH, packaging, brand campaign).

title: Qwen Image Edit 2511 i2i / Reskinning
content:
# Qwen Image Edit 2511 — i2i / Reskinning / Style Transfer

## Use when
Image-to-image transformations where identity, composition, or geometry must survive: photo retouching, wardrobe swap, background swap with face lock, style transfer with structural preservation, character LoRA application, abstract reskin. Edit 2511 (purpose-built i2i) beats base 2512 i2i for everything except very-high-denoise abstract transforms.

## Prompt skeleton
```
Source image: [description].
Edit: [single delta — wardrobe swap / background swap / style migration / etc.].
Preserve: [face, pose, composition, lighting geometry].
Denoise: [tier per use case — see Caps].
```

## Caps (denoise tiers — exceed wrong tier and identity drifts or output won't stylize)
- **0.15-0.30**: micro-retouch (skin/eye/teeth fixes, color grade).
- **0.30-0.50**: wardrobe swap, object replacement, background swap with identity lock.
- **0.50-0.70**: material/style change.
- **0.70-0.85**: medium swap (photo → illustration).
- **0.85-1.00**: abstract transform / silhouette / heavy reskin — use base 2512 i2i here instead; Edit 2511 will fight to preserve pixel structure you're trying to discard.

## Right model per use case
- **Subtle photo retouching (preserve photorealism)**: Edit 2511 @ denoise 0.20-0.35.
- **Heavy stylization / cartoonization / style transfer**: Edit 2511 + style LoRA @ denoise 0.55-0.80. Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Style-Transfer variant is purpose-built.
- **Character LoRA application (i2i)**: Edit 2511 @ denoise per use case. For prompt-only re-generation, use base 2512.
- **High-denoise abstract (photo → silhouette / vector / woodcut)**: base 2512 i2i @ denoise 0.85-1.0. Edit 2511 fights this.

## Reference image prep
- Crop tight on subject for identity edits; pad with neutral background.
- Match aspect to output target — Edit 2511 scales to output resolution.
- 1024-1536 long edge is the sweet spot. Very low-res inputs degrade VL semantic parsing.

## LoRA pairing
- Trigger words should be unique tokens not in base vocabulary (`sks_personname` / `ohwx personname` conventions).
- Mention trigger once early, near subject anchor.
- Stack <= 2-3 LoRAs to avoid concept dilution. Lower individual strengths (0.6-0.8) when stacking.
- Style LoRAs go after subject LoRAs in concept priority.

## Negatives (suppress source-photo artifacts)
"No JPEG compression artifacts, no chromatic aberration, no motion blur from source, no original background bleed-through, no double exposure, no ghost limbs, no preserved logos or text from source." Natural language — Qwen ignores keyword stacks.

## Pull concrete vocab
- Light direction match when re-lighting → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.
- New framing if recomposing → Camera Grammar Reference.
- Any expression change → FACS Reference AU codes.

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Identity, composition, and geometry preserved from source — only the edit line applies. No drift."

## Practical default
Edit 2511 for anything identity- or composition-locked; base 2512 i2i only for high-denoise abstract transforms. Denoise tier per use case (see Caps). Always label reference images. Always include source-artifact suppression in negatives.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
Edit 2511 dual-conditions on Qwen2.5-VL semantic encoder + VAE pixel-level latents — that's why it preserves identity and composition better than base 2512 run in i2i mode. The trade-off: it fights high-denoise abstract transforms where you actually want to discard source structure. Pick the model per use case using the table above.
companions: FACS Facial Expression Reference, Camera Grammar Reference, Lighting Vocabulary Reference
prompt_presets:
Subtle retouch. Source image: ____. Edit: ____. Denoise 0.25. Preserve face, pose, composition, lighting [Lighting Vocab]. Suppress: JPEG artifacts, source background bleed-through. Identity, composition, geometry preserved from source — only the edit line applies.
Background swap with identity lock. Source: ____. Keep face, pose, wardrobe, framing exactly. Change: background to ____. Re-light subject to match new scene [Lighting Vocab direction]. Denoise 0.40. Identity, composition, geometry preserved from source — only the edit line applies.
Style transfer. Content from source image. Apply: ____ style (oil painting / gouache / risograph / cel-shaded). Use Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Style-Transfer LoRA. Denoise 0.65. Preserve composition and identity. Identity, composition, geometry preserved from source — only the edit line applies.
Heavy abstract reskin (photo → silhouette / vector / woodcut). NOTE: use base Qwen 2512 i2i at denoise 0.90, NOT Edit 2511 — Edit 2511 will fight high denoise. Strong style anchor in prompt. Reference at 1024-1536 long edge.

title: FACS Facial Expression Reference
content:
# FACS — Facial Action Coding System (Reference)

## What this is
**Model-agnostic facial expression vocabulary.** Use it to write precise expressions for any image/video model that accepts natural-language or structured prompts (Fibo, Qwen Image Edit, Nano Banana 2/Pro, GPT-image 2, Sora 2 Pro cameos, Veo 3.1 i2v with character refs, LTX 2.3, etc.). Beats English emotion words ("happy", "sad") on precision and stacks cleanly across models.

## The Action Unit (AU) system
FACS (Ekman & Friesen, 1978) numbers each facial muscle movement as an Action Unit. Combinations of AUs produce recognizable emotions. The standard format in prompts: `AU<n>+AU<m>` for combinations, or descriptive form `AU1+AU2 brow raise, AU25 lips part`.

## The AUs that matter most for production prompts

| AU | Movement | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| **AU1** | Inner brow raise | Sadness, concern, curiosity, sincerity |
| **AU2** | Outer brow raise | Surprise, fear, excitement |
| **AU4** | Brow lower | Concentration, anger, confusion |
| **AU5** | Upper lid raise | Surprise, intensity, fear |
| **AU6** | Cheek raise | Duchenne smile component (genuine warmth) |
| **AU7** | Lid tight | Intensity, suspicion, anger |
| **AU9** | Nose wrinkle | Disgust, distaste |
| **AU12** | Lip corner pull | Smile (any kind) |
| **AU14** | Dimpler | Contempt (unilateral), suppressed smirk |
| **AU15** | Lip corner depress | Sadness, contempt |
| **AU17** | Chin raise | Sad, sullen, pout |
| **AU20** | Lip stretch | Fear, terror, extreme tension |
| **AU22** | Lip funnel | Kissing, cooing, soft appeal |
| **AU23** | Lip tighten | Controlled anger, suppression |
| **AU24** | Lip pressor | Repressed emotion, controlled anger |
| **AU25** | Lips part | Speaking, surprise, anticipation |
| **AU26** | Jaw drop | Surprise, shock, awe |
| **AU43** | Eyes closed | Sleep, deep emotion, fatigue |
| **AU45** | Blink | Natural, life — use on animated frames |
| **AU46** | Wink | Playful complicity, conspiratorial charm |
| **AU54** | Head tilt down/side | Curiosity, vulnerability, listening |

## Canonical emotion combinations

| Emotion | AU combination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Genuine smile (Duchenne)** | AU6 + AU12 | AU6 (cheek raise) is what makes a smile read as authentic vs. polite |
| **Social/polite smile** | AU12 alone | Lip corners up without cheek raise |
| **True surprise** | AU1 + AU2 + AU5 + AU26 | Brows up, upper lids raised, jaw drops |
| **Sadness (wistful)** | AU1 + AU15 + AU17 | Inner brow up, lip corners down, chin raised |
| **Sadness (Ekman canonical)** | AU1 + AU4 + AU15 | Adds brow lower — more defeated read, less wistful |
| **Anger** | AU4 + AU5 + AU7 + AU24 | Brow lowered, lids tight, lips pressed |
| **Repressed anger / seething** | AU4 + AU7 + AU23 + AU24 | Brow down, lids tight, lips tightened + pressed — anger held behind a closed mouth |
| **Fear** | AU1 + AU2 + AU4 + AU5 + AU20 + AU26 | Brows up + together, lid raise, lip stretch, jaw drop |
| **Apprehension / dread** | AU1 + AU2 + AU4 + AU7 | Fear precursor — brows up and knitted, lids tight but no jaw drop yet |
| **Disgust** | AU9 + AU15 + AU16 | Nose wrinkle, lip corners down, lower lip down |
| **Contempt** | AU12 + AU14 (one side only) | Unilateral smirk |
| **Smug satisfaction** | AU6 + AU12 + AU14 (unilateral) | Duchenne smile with one dimpler — warmth corrupted by self-satisfaction |
| **Skeptical / side-eye** | AU4 + AU7 + AU14 (unilateral) | Brow down, lid tight, one-sided dimple — "I don't buy it" |
| **Concentration** | AU4 + AU7 | Brow down, lid tight — focused gaze |
| **Curiosity / wondering** | AU1 + AU54 (head tilt) | Inner brow up + head tilt |
| **Awe / wonder** | AU1 + AU2 + AU25 | Brows up, lips part, soft jaw |
| **Excitement** | AU1 + AU2 + AU6 + AU12 + AU25 | Brows up, cheek raise, smile, lips open |
| **Explaining / earnest** | AU4 + AU25 | Slight brow furrow, lips open mid-speech |
| **Playful / silly** | AU12 + AU25 + AU26 + AU19 (tongue) | Open mouth smile, tongue show |
| **Melancholy / tired** | AU1 + AU15 + AU43 partial | Inner brow up, lip corners down, drowsy eyes |
| **Embarrassment / sheepish** | AU6 + AU12 + AU54 + AU15 partial | Smile with head tilt down + slight lip corner depression — "I know I messed up but I'm smiling anyway" |
| **Pleading / imploring** | AU1 + AU4 + AU17 + AU25 | Inner brow up + lowered + chin raise + parted lips — maximum vulnerability stack |
| **Wistful / nostalgic** | AU1 + AU6 partial + AU15 partial | Inner brow up with a soft half-smile fighting a lip corner dip — bittersweet read |
| **Relieved / releasing tension** | AU6 + AU12 + AU17 + AU43 partial | Genuine smile with chin raise and softening lids — exhale-face after stress breaks |
| **Flirtatious / coy** | AU46 (unilateral) + AU6 + AU12 + AU54 | Wink + Duchenne smile + head tilt — conspiratorial warmth |

## How to use in prompts

**Structured (Fibo, JSON-style models):**
```json
"expression": "AU6+AU12 genuine smile, AU25 lips slightly parted"
```

**Natural-language (every other model):**
```
expression: AU1+AU2 brow raise, AU25 lips parted in awe
```

**Combined with directive language:**
```
A close-up of [subject], expressing surprise — AU1+AU2 inner and outer brow raise, AU5 upper lid raise, AU26 jaw drop, eyes wide.
```

## Stacking rules
- **Cap at 2-3 AUs per character per frame.** More than that and the model averages them into a neutral / muddy expression.
- **Use combinations from the table** rather than inventing your own — the canonical combos have higher recognition rates because they appear in real photographic training data.
- **Pair with head pose when needed** — AU54 (head tilt) is a powerful modifier that adds 30%+ to emotion read.
- **Don't repeat AU numbers across speakers in a multi-character scene** — give each character a distinct expression vocabulary so the model doesn't merge them.
- **Unilateral AU notation**: write `AU14 (unilateral)` or `AU46 (unilateral)` when only one side of the face fires (the asymmetry is the read).

## Why this beats English emotion words
- "Happy" → could be any of 5+ smile types; model picks at random
- "AU6+AU12" → specifically a Duchenne smile, model trained on this signal
- "Sad" → ambiguous (crying? brooding? wistful? defeated?)
- "AU1+AU15+AU17" → specifically melancholic wistful sadness; "AU1+AU4+AU15" → defeated Ekman-canonical sadness. Distinct combos, distinct reads.
- "Surprised" → mild surprise vs. shock vs. awe all conflated
- "AU1+AU2+AU5+AU26" → unambiguous full-surprise combo

## Practical default
Pick 1 canonical combo from the table per character per frame. Use the descriptive form (`AU6+AU12 genuine smile`) when writing for natural-language models; use pure-AU form (`AU6+AU12`) inside Fibo's structured_prompt `expression` field. Pair with head pose (`AU54 head tilt right`) for stronger emotion read. Never stack more than 3 AUs per character.
companions: Camera Grammar Reference, Lighting Vocabulary Reference
prompt_presets:
expression: AU6+AU12 genuine smile, AU25 lips slightly parted
expression: AU1+AU2+AU5+AU26 — full surprise (brows up, upper lid raise, jaw drop)
expression: AU1+AU4+AU15 — defeated sadness (Ekman canonical, more weight than wistful AU1+AU15+AU17)
expression: AU4+AU7+AU14 (unilateral) — skeptical side-eye, "I don't buy it"
expression: AU46 (unilateral) + AU6+AU12 + AU54 — flirtatious coy (wink + Duchenne + head tilt)

title: Camera Grammar Reference
content:
# Camera Grammar — Shot, Angle, Movement, Lens (Reference)

## What this is
**Model-agnostic film/camera vocabulary.** Use it to write precise camera direction for any image/video model. The terms below are recognized by Sora 2, Veo 3.1, WAN, Kling, LTX, Seedance, Nano Banana, Qwen, GPT-image, Fibo — all of them respond better to specific cinema language than to vague phrases like "good shot" or "dynamic angle".

## Shot scale (frame size)

| Term | Description | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Extreme wide / Establishing** | Subject tiny or absent, environment dominant | Scene reveals, world scale, location intros |
| **Wide / Long shot** | Full subject visible, environment significant | Character-in-world, action context |
| **Medium-wide / Cowboy** | Subject mid-thigh up | Walking, casual action, two-shot dialogue |
| **Medium** | Subject waist-up | Standard dialogue, interview, hero shots |
| **Medium close-up (MCU)** | Subject chest-up | Performance close-up, slight intimacy |
| **Close-up (CU)** | Face and shoulders | Emotion, dialogue intensity, reaction |
| **Extreme close-up (ECU)** | Detail of face or object | Micro-expression, product detail, intensity |
| **Insert** | Cutaway to specific object/detail | Plot beat, prop emphasis, evidence |
| **Two-shot** | Two subjects in frame | Dialogue, relationship dynamics |
| **Group shot** | 3+ subjects in frame | Ensemble, crowd context |

## Camera angle

| Term | Description | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Eye level** | Camera at subject's eye height | Neutral, default, equal standing |
| **Low angle** | Camera below subject, looking up | Power, scale, heroism, intimidation |
| **High angle** | Camera above subject, looking down | Vulnerability, smallness, overview |
| **Overhead / Bird's eye** | Camera directly above, top-down | Layout, abstract, surveillance |
| **Worm's eye** | Camera at ground looking straight up | Extreme power, monumental |
| **Dutch tilt / Canted** | Camera rotated 10-20° off horizontal | Tension, unease, instability |
| **POV / First-person** | From subject's eye position | Immersion, subjectivity |
| **Over-the-shoulder (OTS)** | Camera behind one subject facing another | Dialogue, relationship, witness |
| **Reverse angle** | Opposite of previous shot's angle | Conversation cuts, perspective shift |
| **Profile / 90°** | Subject viewed from the side | Silhouette, character turnaround |

## Camera movement

| Term | Description | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Static / Locked** | No movement | Composition emphasis, intimate dialogue |
| **Pan** | Horizontal rotation on fixed point | Following lateral action, scanning environment |
| **Tilt** | Vertical rotation on fixed point | Revealing height, looking up/down |
| **Dolly in / Push-in** | Camera physically moves toward subject | Building intensity, focus tightening |
| **Dolly out / Pull-back** | Camera physically moves away | Revealing context, emotional release |
| **Tracking / Trucking** | Camera moves laterally alongside subject | Following motion, character walks |
| **Crane / Jib** | Camera moves vertically + horizontally on arm | Dramatic reveals, scale changes |
| **Orbit / Arc** | Camera circles subject | 3D emphasis, dimensionality |
| **Handheld** | Operator-carried camera | Authenticity, immediacy, documentary |
| **Steadicam** | Smooth handheld with stabilizer | Walking-with-subject, immersive flow |
| **Whip pan** | Rapid horizontal pan | Energy, transition, action |
| **Zoom in/out** | Lens focal-length change | Compressed feel, surveillance, intensity |
| **Rack focus** | Focus shifts between depth planes | Attention transfer, reveal |
| **Dolly zoom / Vertigo** | Dolly in + zoom out (or reverse) | Unease, psychological shift |
| **Aerial / Drone** | Camera flies in 3D space | Establishment, scale, geographic |

## Lens / focal length language

| Term | Field of view | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Ultra-wide (14-24mm)** | Very wide FOV | Environments, immersion, distortion |
| **Wide (28-35mm)** | Wide FOV, mild distortion | Documentary, environmental portrait, scale |
| **Normal (50mm)** | Approximates human vision | Natural perspective, default |
| **Short telephoto (85mm)** | Slightly compressed | Classic portrait, flattering |
| **Telephoto (135-200mm)** | Compressed, isolated subject | Subject separation, sports |
| **Super telephoto (300mm+)** | Heavily compressed | Wildlife, sports, surveillance |
| **Macro (100mm 1:1)** | Extreme close detail | Product, texture, food, nature |
| **Anamorphic (any FL)** | 2.39:1 squeeze + oval bokeh | Cinema look, horizontal lens flares |
| **Tilt-shift** | Plane of focus controlled | Architecture, miniature effect |

## Depth-of-field cues
- **Shallow DOF**: subject sharp, background blurred. Triggers: "f/1.4", "f/2", "shallow depth of field", "creamy bokeh", "subject isolated".
- **Deep DOF**: everything in focus. Triggers: "f/11", "f/16", "deep focus", "everything sharp", "landscape DOF".
- **Rack focus**: focus shifts during the shot from foreground to background.

## Aspect ratio shorthand (use case → ratio)
- Cinema widescreen: 2.39:1 (anamorphic) or 21:9
- Standard widescreen: 16:9
- Classic photo / DSLR: 3:2
- Editorial portrait: 4:5 or 3:4
- Square social: 1:1
- Vertical story / reel: 9:16
- Banner: 4:1 or 8:1
- Vertical strip: 1:4 or 1:8

## How to use in prompts

**Composed shot description (single sentence):**
```
Medium close-up, slight low angle, 85mm portrait lens at f/1.4 with creamy bokeh, slow dolly-in over 4 seconds.
```

**For Fibo / structured models (slot into camera{} block):**
```json
"camera": {
  "angle": "slight low angle, eye-level",
  "framing": "medium close-up",
  "depth_of_field": "shallow, f/1.4",
  "feel": "slow dolly-in"
}
```

## Practical default
For every shot, specify at minimum: shot scale + angle + movement (or "static"). Add lens / DOF when subject separation matters. Add aspect ratio at the end. Don't pile up more than 3 movement directives in one shot — pick one dominant move.
companions: Lighting Vocabulary Reference, FACS Facial Expression Reference
prompt_presets:
Medium close-up, slight low angle, 85mm at f/1.4, shallow depth of field, slow dolly-in
Wide establishing shot, eye level, 35mm, deep focus, static, 16:9
Over-the-shoulder two-shot, 50mm, rack focus from foreground to background
Tracking shot, handheld, medium framing, following subject from left to right

title: Lighting Vocabulary Reference
content:
# Lighting Vocabulary — Direction, Quality, Color, Source (Reference)

## What this is
**Model-agnostic lighting language.** Vague terms like "good lighting" or "cinematic" underperform across every image/video model. Specific lighting direction, quality, source type, and color temperature improve fidelity 30-50% and let you reproduce a look across models.

## The four dimensions to specify

A complete lighting brief covers **direction + quality + source + color**. State all four when the look matters.

### 1. Direction

| Term | Description | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Front light** | Light from camera direction | Flat, even, low drama |
| **Side light (90°)** | Light from camera-left or camera-right | Strong dimension, sculpted face, half-shadow |
| **Three-quarter (45°)** | Light between front and side | Most flattering portrait standard |
| **Back light** | Light from behind subject toward camera | Silhouette, halo, rim |
| **Top light** | Light from directly above | Pool lighting, shadow under eyes, dramatic |
| **Under light** | Light from below | Horror, unnatural, theatrical |
| **Rim / Edge light** | Light grazing the edge of subject | Separation from background, halo |
| **Kicker** | 3/4-back side light | Adds dimensional edge to face/body |
| **Hair light** | Light hitting hair from above-back | Classic Hollywood, separates from BG |

### 2. Quality

| Term | Description | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Hard light** | Sharp shadows, defined edges | Drama, contrast, fashion, noir |
| **Soft light** | Gradual shadow transition | Beauty, warmth, naturalistic portrait |
| **Diffused** | Spread evenly, low contrast | Overcast, north-window, large softbox |
| **Direct** | Unmodified light source | Sun, bare bulb, harsh strobe |
| **Bounced** | Reflected off surface | Naturalistic, even fill |
| **Volumetric** | Visible in atmosphere (fog, dust, smoke) | Atmospheric drama, god-rays |
| **Specular** | Sharp highlights on glossy surfaces | Product, metallic, wet surfaces |

### 3. Source

| Source | Color temp | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Candlelight** | 1900-2200K | Very warm, intimate, low intensity |
| **Tungsten / Incandescent** | 2700-3200K | Warm interior, vintage, cozy |
| **Halogen** | 3000-3400K | Slightly cooler than tungsten |
| **Fluorescent (warm)** | 3000-4000K | Office, retail |
| **Fluorescent (cool)** | 4000-5000K | Industrial, hospital, harsh |
| **Daylight (cloudy)** | 6000-7500K | Overcast, blue-shifted |
| **Daylight (clear)** | 5200-5600K | Sun in open shade, mid-day |
| **Golden hour** | 2500-3500K | Warm directional, low sun, long shadows |
| **Blue hour** | 8000-10000K | Cool ambient, before sunrise / after sunset |
| **Moonlight** | 4100K (perceived blue) | Cool, low intensity, dramatic |
| **Neon / Practical signage** | Mixed (3000-8000K) | Cyberpunk, urban night, mixed color casts |
| **LED panel** | Variable (2700-6500K) | Flexible studio, adjustable |
| **Mixed practicals** | Multiple sources | Realistic interior with lamps + windows |

### 4. Color & mood named patterns

| Pattern | Direction + quality + temp | Mood |
|---|---|---|
| **Golden hour** | Low angle side, warm 2500-3500K, soft | Romance, warmth, nostalgia |
| **Blue hour** | Diffused top, cool 8000K | Mystery, calm, melancholy |
| **High-key** | Even diffused, no shadows | Optimistic, commercial, beauty |
| **Low-key** | Single direction, deep shadows | Drama, noir, mystery |
| **Chiaroscuro** | Single hard light, dark surrounds | Renaissance painting, drama |
| **Rembrandt** | 45° from above creating triangle on cheek | Portrait classic, depth |
| **Split lighting** | Pure 90° side, half face shadow | Tension, duality, drama |
| **Butterfly / Paramount** | Above-camera, small nose shadow | Glamour, fashion, beauty |
| **Loop lighting** | 30-45° from camera | Standard flattering portrait |
| **Broad lighting** | Light on near side of face | Wider face appearance |
| **Short lighting** | Light on far side of face | Slimmer face, dimension |
| **Silhouette** | Pure backlight, no fill | Mystery, scale, drama |
| **Backlit halo** | Strong backlight, soft fill | Romantic, spiritual, hero |
| **Neon noir** | Mixed practicals, magenta + cyan, wet ground | Cyberpunk, urban night |
| **Available light / Documentary** | Whatever's there, no modification | Naturalism, authenticity |
| **Studio flash / Beauty dish** | Direct front from above, fill | Editorial fashion |

## How to specify in prompts

**Full lighting brief (1 sentence):**
```
Soft 45° three-quarter key light from camera-left, warm 3200K tungsten, deep shadows on the right side of the face, no fill.
```

**For Fibo / structured models:**
```json
"lighting": {
  "style": "Rembrandt, warm tungsten",
  "direction": "45° camera-left, slight above",
  "shadows": "deep, defined triangle on right cheek"
}
```

**Compact form for image models:**
```
golden hour, low directional from camera-left, long warm shadows
```

## Lighting + scene matching (for i2i / compositing)
When placing a subject into a new environment via Edit/inpaint:
- Match key light direction first (the most-noticed mismatch)
- Match color temperature second
- Match quality (hard vs soft) third
- Add rim light from the environment's natural direction for separation

```
Re-light subject to match environment's key light (warm 3200K from camera-right at 45°), preserve original facial shadow geometry, add subtle rim from background neon practicals on left.
```

## Gotchas
- "Good lighting" → useless; model picks randomly
- "Cinematic lighting" → too vague unless paired with direction
- Stacking 5+ lighting cues confuses the model; pick 2-3 dominant terms
- "Natural lighting" without time-of-day is ambiguous — say "soft north-window daylight" or "golden hour direct sun"
- Color temperature numbers (Kelvin) help precision but pair with named source for redundancy

## Practical default
Always state direction + quality + source/temperature in three short clauses. Pick from one of the named patterns when the brief is short. Match lighting carefully when compositing — direction first, temperature second, quality third.

Soft 45° three-quarter key from camera-left, warm 3200K tungsten, deep shadows right side
Golden hour, low directional from camera-left, long warm shadows, 2800K
Rembrandt lighting, single hard light 45° above camera-right, deep shadow with triangle on cheek
Mixed practical neon, magenta and cyan, wet ground reflections, cyberpunk noir

title: Qwen Image Edit 2509 fp8 Multi-Angle
content:
# Qwen Image Edit 2509 fp8 — Multi-Angle Scene Creation (Next Scene LoRA)

## Use when
Generating multi-angle camera moves through a scene where **the camera is the protagonist** and characters do minimal action: storyboard sequences of "same scene, new angle", ad-style camera tours of an environment, character intros where framing carries the story. Pairs Qwen Image Edit 2509 fp8 with the Next Scene 2509 LoRA (e.g. lovis93/next-scene-qwen-image-lora-2509). Runs locally in ComfyUI via TextEncodeQwenImageEditPlus.

## Prompt skeleton — camera FIRST, action minimal
```
Next Scene: [camera move + framing — strong LoRA tokens], [WHO is in focus + ONE simple action + ONE emotion cue].
```

Strong camera tokens the LoRA was trained on (bilingual; both forms work, prefer both on one line):
- `将镜头向前/后/左/右移动` / `Move the camera forward / back / left / right`
- `将镜头向上/下移动` / `Move the camera up / down`
- `将镜头向左/右旋转N度` / `Rotate the camera N degrees left / right`
- `将镜头转为广角镜头` / `Turn to a wide-angle lens`
- `将镜头转为特写镜头` / `Turn to a close-up`
- `将镜头转为俯视` / `Turn to a top-down view`
- `smooth tracking shot` / `slow push-in` / `slow dolly-in` / `deliberate camera move`

## Caps — actions and emotion MUST be minimal (otherwise framing breaks)
- Camera direction is the FIRST clause of every line — non-negotiable.
- <= 1 simple action verb per line (hops, turns, raises, leans, looks up).
- <= 1 emotion descriptor per line (excited / curious / nervous / calm).
- <= 1 prop interaction per line; usually zero.
- The entire subject+action+emotion clause is <= 12 words.
- NO multi-sentence character direction. NO complex blocking ("walks across the room while doing X and then Y") — it conflicts with the LoRA's framing signal and degrades both.

## Input contract (continuity across beats)
- Source frame from the previous beat (image input to the Edit pipeline).
- Continuity hint recommended: "the same plush toys", "still on the sofa", "from the earlier shot" — helps the LoRA hold identity + layout.
- **Same-framing beat (camera holds in place)**: drop the camera instruction entirely; write only the minimal action. Example: `Next Scene: 所有人保持在同样的位置，但中间的玩偶转头看向观众 — same positions, central plush turns to look at the viewer.`

## Negatives
"No multi-character orchestration, no complex action choreography, no scene transitions, no environment change, no character introductions unless explicitly stated, no rapid cuts, no over-stylized animation effects, no AI-generated look."

## Pull concrete vocab
- Camera direction tokens above are the LoRA's trained grammar — use them verbatim. Underlying shot type/angle terms → Camera Grammar Reference.
- Lighting changes → Lighting Vocabulary Reference (use sparingly — lighting is best held constant across multi-angle beats).
- Expression cues → FACS Reference, but stick to ONE AU code per line (e.g. AU12 smile, AU1+AU2 surprise).

## LoRA strength tuning
- If character actions start to override framing: **lower Next Scene LoRA strength** and add more cinematic camera language ("smooth tracking shot", "slow push-in").
- If framing locks but characters look frozen: raise strength slightly and add ONE emotion word per line.

## Bookend (restate at end of any sequence prompt or final line)
"Camera is the protagonist — actions remain minimal. Identity and environment preserved across angles."

## Practical default
Camera chunk FIRST in the string node feeding `TextEncodeQwenImageEditPlus`. Character direction is a brief tail clause, never the lead. Bilingual (zh+en) on the same line. One action verb + one emotion word per line, <= 12 words for the subject+action clause. Reference previous frame's subjects by continuity hint. Tune LoRA strength to balance framing vs. action.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
The Next Scene 2509 LoRA was trained on "same scene, new angle" data — its strength is reading camera tokens and generating coherent multi-angle output. It treats heavy character direction as conflict with the framing signal and degrades both. The minimal-action discipline is what unlocks the LoRA's value. For complex character action, use Qwen Image Edit 2511 (newer Edit variant, separate row) or a video model — not this row.

title: Nano Banana Pro Character Sheet Creation
content:
# Nano Banana Pro — Character Sheet Creation (industry-standard turnarounds, expression sheets, pose sheets)

## Use when
Producing production-grade character reference sheets for animation, comics, game characters, brand mascots, or asset libraries: turnaround multi-angle sheets, expression sheets, pose sheets, color callouts, detail close-ups. Pro outperforms Flash 2 here because dense multi-panel composition + in-pixel text labels (view names, color hex, FACS codes) + identity preservation across panels is exactly what Pro is built for.

## Prompt skeleton
```
Generate a character sheet for [NAME] (identity locked from Image 1).
Sheet type: [turnaround / expression / pose / color callout / construction].
Layout: [N panels, arrangement — "5 views left-to-right" or "3x3 grid"].
Per-panel spec:
  Panel 1: [view spec — front 0° / 3/4 45° / profile 90° / 3/4 back 135° / back 180° for turnaround] · label "____"
  Panel 2: [same shape — view OR AU codes OR pose name] · label "____"
  ...
Background: plain neutral [warm gray RGB ~#C8C5BE / cream / studio white], no shadows below, no environment elements.
Lighting: flat diffused studio light, even from all sides, no directional shadows on subject.
Scale: subject occupies identical frame height in every panel — "constant ~80% panel height".
Identity locked from Image 1 — face, hair, proportions, wardrobe, accessories exactly across every panel.
```

## Caps (exceed → identity drift, panel collision, label crowding)
- <= 5 views in a turnaround (front / 3/4 / profile / 3/4 back / back).
- <= 9 panels in a 3x3 expression sheet (industry standard).
- <= 6 panels in a pose sheet.
- <= 1 label per panel; cap label length at 4 words.
- Constant scale across panels — non-negotiable.
- ONE reference image is the identity anchor.
- ONE sheet type per generation — don't mix turnaround + expressions in one call (drift compounds).

## Industry-standard sheet types

| Sheet | Standard panels | Aspect | Production use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Turnaround** | 4-5 views: front 0°, 3/4 45°, profile 90°, [3/4 back 135°], back 180° | 21:9 wide or 16:9 | Animation / 3D modeling rig reference |
| **Expression sheet** | 9 panels in 3x3: neutral + 8 FACS-coded emotions | 1:1 or 4:5 | Emotion range library |
| **Pose sheet** | 6 full-body poses: idle, walk, run, gesture A, gesture B, action | 16:9 | Motion / pose library |
| **Color callout** | Single front view + 6-10 color swatches with hex/name labels | 4:5 | Production color script |
| **Detail close-ups** | 4-6 zoomed details: face, hands, weapon, accessory, distinguishing mark | 1:1 grid | Production detail reference |
| **Construction sheet** | Side profile with head-height proportion lines (8-head convention) | 3:4 | Rigging / proportion reference |

## Input contract
- Image 1: master character reference (single canonical pose, neutral expression, plain background, clean lighting).
- Optional Image 2: wardrobe variant or hair-detail reference.
- Optional Image 3: prop / accessory reference.

## Preserve / change (everything-preserve)
```
Preserve from Image 1 — exactly across every panel:
  • Face: eye shape and color, nose, lips, jawline, distinguishing facial features.
  • Hair: color, length, texture, style.
  • Skin: tone, freckles, markings, scars.
  • Body: proportions, height (relative scale), build, posture defaults.
  • Wardrobe: every garment, accessory, color, material, fit.
  • Accessories: every prop, jewelry, eyewear with exact placement.
Change only: the view angle / expression / pose / detail crop per panel as specified.
```

## Pull concrete vocab
- Each expression panel → FACS Reference AU codes (use canonical combinations — AU6+AU12 for genuine smile, AU1+AU2+AU5+AU26 for surprise, etc.).
- View angles → Camera Grammar Reference (front, 3/4, profile, back; eye-level for turnarounds).
- Flat-studio lighting setup → Lighting Vocabulary Reference (high-key, even diffused, no directional shadows).

## Negatives
"No scale drift between panels, no outfit drift, no accessory drift, no proportion shift, no hairstyle drift, no skin-tone shift, no background substitution, no environmental elements, no directional shadows on subject, no contact shadow below the figure, no label mutation, no extra unrequested panels, no AI-generated look."

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Identity locked from Image 1 across every panel — proportions, wardrobe, hair, color exactly. Constant scale, constant flat lighting, plain neutral background. Each panel is the same character; only [view/expression/pose] varies. No drift across panels."

## Practical default
Industry-standard turnaround: 4-5 views in one 21:9 frame, constant scale, flat diffused light, plain neutral background, view-name labels under each panel. Industry-standard expression sheet: 9 expressions in 3x3, FACS-coded, same character, same lighting. Pro Thinking level High. 4K for production reference; 2K for proofs. Always run a separate color-callout pass per character.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
Character sheets are the canonical reference asset for any animation, comic, game, or brand-mascot pipeline. Pro's strengths — dense multi-panel composition, in-pixel typography for labels, identity preservation across views — make it the right pick over Flash 2 or single-image generators. The industry-standard 3-artifact minimum per character (turnaround + expression sheet + color callout) is what unlocks downstream pipelines (LoRA training, 3D modeling, animation rigging). Pair with World Building context once the sheet is locked to place the character in scenes.

# GPT-image 2 — Character Sheet Creation (industry-standard turnarounds, expression sheets, pose sheets)

## Use when
Producing production-grade character reference sheets for animation, comics, game characters, brand mascots, or asset libraries. GPT-image 2's reasoning pass + best-in-class text rendering + multi-panel consistency (up to 8 panels in one prompt with a single reference) make it the right pick when sheet labels (view names, FACS codes, color hex) must hold up at production grade.

## Prompt skeleton
```
INPUT: Image 1 — character master reference (label this explicitly).

TASK: Generate a character sheet for [NAME].
Sheet type: [turnaround / expression / pose / color callout / construction].
Layout: [N panels, arrangement].
Per-panel spec:
  Panel 1: [view spec or AU codes or pose name] · label "____"
  Panel 2: ____
  ...
Background: plain neutral [warm gray / cream / studio white], no shadows below, no environment.
Lighting: flat diffused studio light, even from all sides, no directional shadows on subject.
Scale: subject same frame height in every panel — "constant ~80% panel height".
Labels: in quotes under each panel.

size="1536x1024" (turnarounds, poses) OR "1024x1536" (expression sheets vertical, color callouts). quality="high".

PRESERVE: face, hair, body proportions, wardrobe, accessories, color palette from Image 1 — exactly across every panel.
```

## Caps (exceed → identity drift, panel collision)
- <= 8 panels in a single sheet (GPT-image 2's native consistency cap per prompt).
- <= 5 views in a turnaround.
- <= 9 panels in a 3x3 expression sheet (use n=2 for 18 if needed — splits across calls).
- <= 1 label per panel; cap label length at 4 words.
- Constant scale across panels — non-negotiable.
- ONE reference image is the identity anchor.
- ONE sheet type per generation.

## Industry-standard sheet types

| Sheet | Standard panels | Aspect | Production use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Turnaround** | 4-5 views: front 0°, 3/4 45°, profile 90°, [3/4 back 135°], back 180° | 21:9 / 16:9 wide (1536x1024) | Animation / 3D rig reference |
| **Expression sheet** | 9 panels in 3x3: neutral + 8 FACS-coded emotions | 1:1 / 4:5 (1024x1536) | Emotion range library |
| **Pose sheet** | 6 full-body poses: idle, walk, run, gesture A/B, action | 16:9 (1536x1024) | Motion library |
| **Color callout** | Single front view + 6-10 color swatches with hex/name labels | 4:5 (1024x1536) | Production color script |
| **Detail close-ups** | 4-6 zoomed details: face, hands, prop, accessory | 1:1 grid (1024x1024) | Production detail reference |
| **Construction sheet** | Side profile with head-height proportion lines (8-head convention) | 3:4 (1024x1536) | Rigging / proportion reference |

## Input contract
- Image 1: master character reference (single canonical pose, neutral expression, plain background, clean lighting). **Label explicitly**: "Image 1 is the character master reference."
- Optional Image 2: wardrobe variant. Optional Image 3: prop/accessory.
- For each input, state its role in the prompt — GPT-image 2's reasoning pass needs the role tags to map references correctly.

## Preserve / change (everything-preserve, exhaustive)
```
Preserve from Image 1 — exactly across every panel:
  • Face: facial structure, eye shape and color, nose, lips, jawline, brow shape.
  • Hair: color, length, texture, style, parting.
  • Skin: tone, freckles, markings, scars, micro-features.
  • Body: proportions, height (relative scale), build, posture defaults.
  • Wardrobe: every garment, accessory, color, material, drape, fit.
  • Accessories: every prop, jewelry, eyewear with exact placement.
  • Distinguishing features: scars, tattoos, prosthetics, markings.
Change only: the view angle / expression / pose / detail crop as specified per panel.
```

## Pull concrete vocab
- Expression panels → FACS Reference (canonical AU combinations — AU6+AU12 smile, AU1+AU2+AU5+AU26 surprise, etc.).
- View angles → Camera Grammar Reference (front 0°, 3/4 45°, profile 90°, 3/4 back 135°, back 180°; eye-level).
- Flat-studio lighting setup → Lighting Vocabulary Reference (high-key, even diffused, no directional, no contact shadow).

## Negatives
"No scale drift between panels, no outfit drift, no accessory drift, no proportion shift, no hairstyle drift, no skin-tone shift, no background substitution, no environmental elements, no directional shadows on subject, no contact shadow below the figure, no label mutation, no extra unrequested panels."

## Settings (GPT-image 2 specific)
- size: 1536x1024 (turnarounds, poses), 1024x1536 (vertical expression sheets, color callouts), 1024x1024 (detail close-up grids)
- quality: "high" — mandatory for sheets; small labels and panel consistency degrade at lower quality
- For batch character variants (same character, different wardrobes): n=4 or n=8 with preserved identity language

## Bookend (restate at end)
"Identity locked from Image 1 across every panel — face, proportions, wardrobe, accessories, color exactly. Constant scale, constant flat lighting, plain neutral background. Each panel is the same character; only [view/expression/pose] varies. No drift across panels."

## Practical default
Industry-standard turnaround: 4-5 views in one 1536x1024 frame, constant scale, flat diffused studio light, plain neutral background, view-name labels under each panel. quality="high" mandatory. Pair with separate 3x3 expression sheet (1024x1536) and color callout (1024x1536, front view + labeled swatches) for a production-grade 3-artifact reference set per character.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
GPT-image 2's reasoning pass handles "same character, varied view" cleanly — the model can hold identity across up to 8 panels in one prompt with a single reference. Best-in-class label rendering means the sheet can carry view names, FACS codes, color hex values without garbling. Compared to Nano Banana Pro Character Sheet: GPT-image 2 wins on text-rendering precision and on bilingual/multilingual labels; Pro wins on visual consistency at the highest panel counts (8+). Pick GPT-image 2 here when labels are load-bearing (color scripts, FACS-coded expression sheets, construction sheets with measurements).

title: Qwen 2512 Production Portraits
content:
# Qwen 2512 — Production Portraits & Character Consistency

## Use when
Production-grade character work: portraits, editorial figures, fashion / lifestyle, multi-shot character consistency. Covers both pure t2i (Qwen 2512 base) and reference-driven workflows (Qwen Image Edit 2511 when one or more reference images are involved). Pick this row when the brief is "this person, in this shot, lit this way" — not when you need slide/chart text (Qwen 2512 Production) or environment composition (Qwen Image Edit 2511 World Building).

## Prompt skeleton — action first, then character, then polish
```
[ACTION + SHOT TYPE]. [COMPOSITION + LENS + ANGLE + DOF].
Use reference image 1 for [identity role]. Use reference image 2 for [secondary role].
Preserve [exact traits that must not drift].
[LIGHTING — source + direction + temperature]. [MATERIALS + TEXTURES]. [FINAL LOOK].
```

Mental model: **define the shot → define the person → define the polish**. Qwen responds better when the action lands first and character features come after, rather than front-loading every facial detail at the start.

## Input contract — multi-reference variant (Edit 2511 only)
- **t2i base (Qwen 2512)** accepts NO reference images. Identity must be carried by a trained LoRA + a unique trigger token in the prompt (e.g. `Marella`). Reference instructions in the prompt have no effect on a pure t2i call.
- **Edit 2511 i2i** accepts 1–3 reference images. **Always label each input by role**: face / identity, outfit / wardrobe, pose, style, environment. "Use the image" alone underperforms; "Use reference image 1 for facial identity and expression" lands.
- **Face crops** as the identity reference outperform full-body references for non-close-up shots — when the output framing is wider than the reference, feed a tight face crop so the model anchors identity.

## Preserve / change (Edit 2511 — exhaustive)
```
Preserve from Image 1 (identity): facial structure, age, skin tone, eye shape and color, hairline.
Preserve from Image 2 (wardrobe): every garment, color, material, fit.
Only change: pose, lighting, background, framing per the action line.
```

## Caps (exceed → drift, mushy output)
- **≤ 3 references per call** (Edit 2511 hard cap).
- **One main action per prompt** — chained actions ("walking AND turning AND looking up") split focus.
- **One dominant style mode** — photoreal OR illustration, never both.
- **≤ 2 named style influences**. Era + medium + publication >> single artist name.
- **≤ 3 FACS units per expression**. Pair with head pose when needed (AU54 head tilt).
- **Prompt length 40–80 words for portraits, 80–120 words for editorial complexity**. Past 120, the trailing clauses lose weight.

## Camera vocabulary that lands (production-direct)
Be explicit like a DP brief, not "cinematic" alone:
- **Shot type**: wide / medium-wide / medium / medium close-up / close-up / extreme close-up
- **Angle**: eye-level / slight low / low / high / overhead / over-the-shoulder / three-quarter / strict profile
- **Lens**: 35mm wide-environmental · 50mm normal · 85mm portrait · 100mm macro · 135mm telephoto compression
- **DOF**: shallow at f/1.4–f/2.8 · deep at f/8–f/16 · "sharp focus on the eyes, soft background"
- **Lighting source + direction**: "soft north-window daylight from camera-left at 5600K" · "warm golden-hour key, 3200K, rim light from behind"

## High-quality production language (use sparingly, with concrete cues)
Skin: "natural skin texture, visible pores, micro-imperfections, no plastic finish."
Materials: "crisp fabric weave", "brushed metal", "soft velvet", "glass reflections", "matte paper grain."
Grading: "controlled contrast, subtle highlight roll-off, restrained color palette, editorial finish."
Look: "premium editorial", "luxury advertising", "1990s National Geographic documentary", "Y2K club flyer". Never "ultra masterpiece best quality 4k 8k" — Qwen ignores adjective stacks.

## Pull concrete vocab
- Shot scale + angle + lens + DOF → Camera Grammar Reference.
- Light direction + quality + Kelvin temperature + named patterns (Rembrandt / butterfly / split / golden / blue hour) → Lighting Vocabulary Reference.
- Facial expressions → FACS Reference (e.g. `AU6+AU12 genuine smile`, `AU1+AU2+AU5+AU26 surprise`).

## Negatives
Natural language only (Qwen ignores keyword stacks): "no waxy skin, no over-smoothed face, no plastic look, no extra fingers, no distorted eyes, no AI-generated look, no watermark, no logos, no stylized rendering when photoreal is the goal, no mode bleed between photo and illustration."

For Edit 2511 reference work, also: "no identity drift, no face morph, no wardrobe change unless specified, no environment substitution."

## Settings
- t2i base: CFG 3.5–4 for photoreal, 4–5 for illustration; 28–35 steps; aspect matched to use case.
- Edit 2511 i2i with character refs: denoise 0.35–0.60 for identity-locked pose / wardrobe / background swaps; below that for micro-retouch.

## Bookend (restate at end of every prompt)
"Identity, proportions, and wardrobe locked exactly per the reference; only [the named delta] changes." (Or for pure t2i: "Photoreal mode locked — natural skin texture, no plastic, no AI-generated look.")

## Practical default
Define shot first (action + composition + lens). Then character (identity-lock prefix or labeled refs + preserve list). Then polish (light + materials + finish). One action, one mode, one main subject. Pair with the trained character LoRA + trigger token for cross-shot consistency. Camera + light vocab from the reference rows, not free invention.

---
## Why this context (rationale)
Qwen Image 2512 (base) is t2i only — character consistency on that path comes from a trained character LoRA + a unique trigger token, NOT from reference images (the API doesn't accept them). The same brief on Qwen Image Edit 2511 unlocks 1–3 reference images for identity-locked pose / wardrobe / background swaps. This row covers the production-grade prompt grammar that works on both paths: shot-first → character-then → polish-last structure, explicit DP-level camera language, named lighting, labeled reference roles when refs are used, and natural-language negatives. Use this row when the deliverable is "this specific person, this shot, this finish" — for ensemble or environment-heavy scenes, switch to World Building; for slide/chart text, use Qwen 2512 Production.
